Prior work, such as that of Wei et al., demonstrated these phenomena under model and data scaling, with transitions revealed after applying a log scale to training compute. In this work, we ask three complementary questions: (1) Are phase transitions unique to large models, or can they also be observed in small transformer-based language models? (2) Can such transitions be detected directly in linear training space, rather than only after log rescaling? and (3) Can these transitions emerge at early stages of training? To investigate, we train a small GPT-style transformer on a character-level corpus and analyze the evolution of vocabulary usage throughout training. We track the average word length, the number of correct versus incorrect words, and shifts in vocabulary diversity. Building on these measures, we apply Poisson and sub-Poisson statistics to quantify how words connect and reorganize. This combined analysis reveals a distinct transition point during training. Notably, these transitions are not apparent in standard loss or validation curves, but become visible through our vocabulary- and statistics-based probes. Our findings suggest that phase-transition reorganizations are a general feature of language model training, observable even in modest models, detectable directly in linear training space, and occurring surprisingly early as coherence emerges. This perspective provides new insight into the nonlinear dynamics of language model training and underscores the importance of tailored metrics for uncovering phase transition behaviors

papers.title: Phase Transitions between Accuracy Regimes in L2 regularized Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can phase transitions in L2 regularized deep neural networks be explained geometrically, and can this geometric perspective explain the phenomenon of grokking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric explanation of phase transitions in L2 regularized deep neural networks using Ricci curvature, predicts additional transitions with increased data complexity, and explains grokking as a hysteresis effect due to first-order phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates phase transitions in L2-regularized neural networks linked to geometric change-points in the error landscape, and provides a mechanistic explanation of grokking as hysteresis due to first-order phase transitions.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing L2 regularization causes a first-order phase transition (onset-of-learning) in DNNs, visible as a jump in error and curvature.
Additional phase transitions occur when data complexity is increased, corresponding to geometric change-points in the error landscape.
The Ricci scalar curvature shows sudden changes at transition points, linking geometry to accuracy phases.
Grokking is reproduced as a hysteresis effect where models initialized in low-accuracy phases take many epochs to escape to high-accuracy phases.
The number of transitions increases with data complexity, as demonstrated with MNIST classification.
papers.limitation:
Cannot deduce details on the global structure of the error landscape; cannot guarantee detection of all phases and change-points.
Lack of rigorous bounds on the number of local minima and schemes to avoid hysteresis effects.
future_direction: Develop rigorous bounds on numbers of local minima and schemes to avoid hysteresis.
Investigate error basins linked to accuracy phases and better understand global error geometry.
Develop new probing methods for the intrinsic structure of DNNs beyond L2 regularization.
papers.abstract: Increasing the L2 regularization of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) causes a first-order phase transition into the under-parametrized phase -- the so-called onset-of learning. We explain this transition via the scalar (Ricci) curvature of the error landscape. We predict new transition points as the data complexity is increased and, in accordance with the theory of phase transitions, the existence of hysteresis effects. We confirm both predictions numerically. Our results provide a natural explanation of the recently discovered phenomenon of '\emph{grokking}' as DNN models getting stuck in a local minimum of the error surface, corresponding to a lower accuracy phase. Our work paves the way for new probing methods of the intrinsic structure of DNNs in and beyond the L2 context.

papers.title: Emergence of Separable Manifolds in Deep Language Representations
papers.research_question: How do linguistic category manifolds (e.g., for part-of-speech tags) emerge and become linearly separable across the layers of transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linguistic manifolds emerge across layers in transformer language models, and their linear separability is driven by reduction in manifold radius, dimensionality, and inter-manifold correlations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language manifolds emerge across layers in deep neural networks for NLP, similar to untangling in sensory systems, and the manifold capacity framework provides geometric evidence for this emergence.
papers.key_findings:
Word and linguistic category manifolds become more separable across layers in the masked (predictive) regime.
In the unmasked (contextualizing) regime, word manifolds become less separable, but linguistic manifolds are counteracted by contextualization and show better separation.
POS manifolds emerge most strongly when words are ambiguous (have multiple POS tags).
POS manifolds interpolate between word-like geometry and separable contextual geometry depending on the number of words in each POS class.
Fine-tuning on POS task increases separability of POS manifolds and transfers to other linguistic tasks.
future_direction: Explore the relation between representation geometry and regression performance for tasks like dependency depth.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown much empirical success in solving perceptual tasks across various cognitive modalities. While they are only loosely inspired by the biological brain, recent studies report considerable similarities between representations extracted from task-optimized DNNs and neural populations in the brain. DNNs have subsequently become a popular model class to infer computational principles underlying complex cognitive functions, and in turn, they have also emerged as a natural testbed for applying methods originally developed to probe information in neural populations. In this work, we utilize mean-field theoretic manifold analysis, a recent technique from computational neuroscience that connects geometry of feature representations with linear separability of classes, to analyze language representations from large-scale contextual embedding models. We explore representations from different model families (BERT, RoBERTa, GPT, etc.) and find evidence for emergence of linguistic manifolds across layer depth (e.g., manifolds for part-of-speech tags), especially in ambiguous data (i.e, words with multiple part-of-speech tags, or part-of-speech classes including many words). In addition, we find that the emergence of linear separability in these manifolds is driven by a combined reduction of manifolds' radius, dimensionality and inter-manifold correlations.

papers.title: Statistical Physics of Deep Neural Networks: Generalization Capability, Beyond the Infinite Width, and Feature Learning
papers.research_question: This thesis investigates three interconnected questions: (1) Can we derive an improved asymptotic bound on the generalization performance of DNNs? (2) How do DNNs behave in a thermodynamic limit where the number of training examples scales with the number of neurons per layer? (3) Do DNNs truly learn dataset features or merely memorize them?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis contributes three main results: (1) an improved asymptotic bound on generalization error that depends only on the last layer size, (2) a statistical mechanics framework for DNNs in a proportional regime beyond the infinite width limit, linking them to Student's t-processes, and (3) a task-explicit analysis showing conditions under which DNNs learn dataset features rather than memorizing.
papers.conclusion: The thesis demonstrates that statistical physics methods can provide significant insights into the generalization, behavior in proportional regimes, and feature learning of DNNs, contributing to more interpretable AI.
papers.key_findings:
An asymptotic generalization bound that depends only on the last layer size, improving classical statistical learning theory bounds.
A closed formula for the generalization error of a finite-width one-hidden layer network in the proportional regime.
An approximate expression for the partition function of deep neural networks in the proportional regime.
A link between deep neural networks in the proportional regime and Student's t-processes.
Evidence that DNNs can learn dataset features rather than memorizing, as shown by analyzing the volume of the solution space and Gaussianity breaking.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at many tasks, often rivaling or surpassing human performance. Yet their internal processes remain elusive, frequently described as "black boxes." While performance can be refined experimentally, achieving a fundamental grasp of their inner workings is still a challenge. Statistical Mechanics has long tackled computational problems, and this thesis applies physics-based insights to understand DNNs via three complementary approaches. First, by averaging over data, we derive an asymptotic bound on generalization that depends solely on the size of the last layer, rather than on the total number of parameters -- revealing how deep architectures process information differently across layers. Second, adopting a data-dependent viewpoint, we explore a finite-width thermodynamic limit beyond the infinite-width regime. This leads to: (i) a closed-form expression for the generalization error in a finite-width one-hidden-layer network (regression task); (ii) an approximate partition function for deeper architectures; and (iii) a link between deep networks in this thermodynamic limit and Student's t-processes. Finally, from a task-explicit perspective, we present a preliminary analysis of how DNNs interact with a controlled dataset, investigating whether they truly internalize its structure -- collapsing to the teacher -- or merely memorize it. By understanding when a network must learn data structure rather than just memorize, it sheds light on fostering meaningful internal representations. In essence, this thesis leverages the synergy between Statistical Physics and Machine Learning to illuminate the inner behavior of DNNs.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: The Geometry of Neural Nets' Parameter Spaces Under Reparametrization
papers.research_question: How can invariance under reparametrization be achieved in neural networks by explicitly representing the Riemannian metric and following proper transformation rules?
papers.core_contribution: Invariance under reparametrization is an inherent property of neural networks if the Riemannian metric is explicitly represented and the correct transformation rules for geometric objects are followed, resolving inconsistencies in flatness measures, optimization trajectories, and probability densities.
papers.conclusion: By explicitly acknowledging the implicit Riemannian metric and adhering to the associated transformation rules, invariance under reparametrization is guaranteed, providing a geometric framework compatible with existing work on neural network analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Hessian-based flatness measures become invariant under reparametrization when the Hessian is considered as a linear map with the metric (E = G^{-1}H), making its determinant, trace, and eigenvalues invariant.
Gradient descent with any metric is invariant under reparametrization if the metric is explicitly transformed according to geometric rules, not just the chain rule.
Modes of probability densities are invariant when using the Riemannian volume form induced by the metric, generalizing the standard Lebesgue measure.
The Laplace marginal likelihood is invariant under reparametrization when derived with proper geometric transformations.
Preconditioned optimizers like ADAM find sharper minima than SGD when the geometry of the parameter space is accounted for via the Hessian operator E.
papers.limitation: The work focuses on reparametrization consistency and leaves geometric analysis for invariance under symmetry as future work.
future_direction: Geometric analysis for invariance under symmetry
Extending autodiff libraries to automatically handle invariant transformation rules of geometric objects
Constructing non-trivial infinite-width neural networks in a Bayesian way by varying model architecture and prior
papers.abstract: Model reparametrization, which follows the change-of-variable rule of calculus, is a popular way to improve the training of neural nets. But it can also be problematic since it can induce inconsistencies in, e.g., Hessian-based flatness measures, optimization trajectories, and modes of probability densities. This complicates downstream analyses: e.g. one cannot definitively relate flatness with generalization since arbitrary reparametrization changes their relationship. In this work, we study the invariance of neural nets under reparametrization from the perspective of Riemannian geometry. From this point of view, invariance is an inherent property of any neural net if one explicitly represents the metric and uses the correct associated transformation rules. This is important since although the metric is always present, it is often implicitly assumed as identity, and thus dropped from the notation, then lost under reparametrization. We discuss implications for measuring the flatness of minima, optimization, and for probability-density maximization. Finally, we explore some interesting directions where invariance is useful.

papers.title: Critical Phase Transition in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Are qualitative changes in Large Language Models, such as those induced by varying the temperature parameter, phase transitions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a phase transition occurs in practical LLMs when varying the temperature parameter, with critical behaviors similar to those in natural languages.
papers.conclusion: The extensive statistical analysis suggests that a phase transition occurs in LLMs when varying the temperature parameter, providing a meaningful analogy between LLMs and natural phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
A phase transition occurs at a critical temperature Tc ≈ 1, separating a low-temperature regime with repetitive structures from a high-temperature regime where generated sentences are often incomprehensible.
Near the critical point, sequences exhibit critical behaviors such as a power-law decay of correlation and slow convergence toward the stationary state.
Natural language datasets (OpenWebTextCorpus, WikiText) show critical properties similar to LLM-generated sequences at the transition temperature, suggesting LLMs are closest to natural language at criticality.
The low-temperature phase is ordered with chaotic repetitive structures (many peaks in power spectra), while the high-temperature phase is not simply disordered despite finite integrated correlation.
The phase transition is observed across different models (GPT-2, Japanese GPT-2, Pythia) and different mappings (POS tags, characters), indicating robustness.
papers.limitation:
The size of the models analyzed is moderate (70M, 124M, and 361M). Analysis of larger models is important because the true phase transition seems to exist in the large context window limit.
Further investigation is needed to better understand how the criticality relates to linguistic properties and practical tasks.
future_direction: Statistical analysis of larger models to confirm the phase transition in the large context window limit.
Precisely estimating the set of critical exponents for GPT-2, other LLMs, and multiple natural language corpora to classify the universality class.
Studying the potential phase transition at very low temperature between repetitive and deterministic phases.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance. To understand their behaviors, we need to consider the fact that LLMs sometimes show qualitative changes. The natural world also presents such changes called phase transitions, which are defined by singular, divergent statistical quantities. Therefore, an intriguing question is whether qualitative changes in LLMs are phase transitions. In this work, we have conducted extensive analysis on texts generated by LLMs and suggested that a phase transition occurs in LLMs when varying the temperature parameter. Specifically, statistical quantities have divergent properties just at the point between the low-temperature regime, where LLMs generate sentences with clear repetitive structures, and the high-temperature regime, where generated sentences are often incomprehensible. In addition, critical behaviors near the phase transition point, such as a power-law decay of correlation and slow convergence toward the stationary state, are similar to those in natural languages. Our results suggest a meaningful analogy between LLMs and natural phenomena.

papers.title: Predictive learning as a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations
papers.research_question: Does learning to predict future observations cause neural networks to extract low-dimensional latent structure from their sensory inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Predictive learning in neural networks leads to the emergence of low-dimensional internal representations that linearly encode the latent variables of the environment, a process that can be quantified using novel metrics like latent signal transfer and dimensionality gain.
papers.conclusion: Predictive learning is a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations from high-dimensional sensory inputs, which can be characterized by the introduced metrics and analytical tools.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive learning causes neural networks to form low-dimensional representations that map the latent structure of the sensory environment.
Latent space signal transfer occurs during learning, where latent variables become increasingly linearly decodable from the top principal components of the neural representation.
Dimensionality gain (the ratio of linear to nonlinear dimensionality) increases during predictive learning, indicating the extraction of a low-dimensional manifold from high-dimensional observations.
Predictive learning leads to the emergence of neurons with localized activations on the manifold (manifold cells).
Representations formed by predictive learning are more structured and better reflect the latent space than those formed by autoencoding (non-predictive learning).
future_direction: Further testing of the predictive learning framework in neural data.
Application of the framework to additional tasks beyond spatial exploration and arm-reaching.
Investigation of predictive learning as a general principle for representation formation in both biological and artificial neural networks.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have recently achieved many successes in solving sequential processing and planning tasks. Their success is often ascribed to the emergence of the task's low-dimensional latent structure in the network activity - i.e., in the learned neural representations. Here, we investigate the hypothesis that a means for generating representations with easily accessed low-dimensional latent structure, possibly reflecting an underlying semantic organization, is through learning to predict observations about the world. Specifically, we ask whether and when network mechanisms for sensory prediction coincide with those for extracting the underlying latent variables. Using a recurrent neural network model trained to predict a sequence of observations we show that network dynamics exhibit low-dimensional but nonlinearly transformed representations of sensory inputs that map the latent structure of the sensory environment. We quantify these results using nonlinear measures of intrinsic dimensionality and linear decodability of latent variables, and provide mathematical arguments for why such useful predictive representations emerge. We focus throughout on how our results can aid the analysis and interpretation of experimental data.

papers.title: The Origins of Representation Manifolds in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are features represented as manifolds in large language models, and how does cosine similarity in representation space relate to the intrinsic geometry of features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical framework to explain representation manifolds in LLMs, showing that under the continuous correspondence hypothesis, cosine similarity encodes the intrinsic geometry of features through shortest paths on the manifold, and validates this on text embeddings and token activations.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a formal mathematical framework to explain and interpret representation manifolds in large language models, validating the theory on internal representations and text embeddings, and revealing unexpected encodings of distances.
papers.key_findings:
Representation manifolds in LLMs reflect the topology of features (e.g., colors and dates form loops, years form a curve) as predicted by the continuous correspondence hypothesis.
Cosine similarity between feature representations locally reflects distance in the feature metric space, implying isometry up to scaling.
Years in GPT2-small are encoded on a logarithmic scale rather than linear, with larger distances between more recent years.
For colors in text-embedding-large-3, the representations follow a hue cycle rather than other possible encodings like RGB.
The manifold geometry allows linear computation of functions of the feature value, supporting the superposition hypothesis.
papers.limitation:
The hypothesis-driven approach is manual and not scalable, relying on a reasonable starting hypothesis for the metric space.
PCA may not capture the full complexity of distances encoded by the language model, which might be more complex and not correspond to human understanding.
Estimating manifolds in the presence of noise is statistically difficult, and the K-nearest-neighbour graph approach is prone to short-circuits causing errors.
future_direction: Learning the metric automatically rather than manual hypothesis
Developing 'manifold-aware' sparse autoencoders
Using the metric space formalism in future scientific discourse
papers.abstract: There is a large ongoing scientific effort in mechanistic interpretability to map embeddings and internal representations of AI systems into human-understandable concepts. A key element of this effort is the linear representation hypothesis, which posits that neural representations are sparse linear combinations of `almost-orthogonal' direction vectors, reflecting the presence or absence of different features. This model underpins the use of sparse autoencoders to recover features from representations. Moving towards a fuller model of features, in which neural representations could encode not just the presence but also a potentially continuous and multidimensional value for a feature, has been a subject of intense recent discourse. We describe why and how a feature might be represented as a manifold, demonstrating in particular that cosine similarity in representation space may encode the intrinsic geometry of a feature through shortest, on-manifold paths, potentially answering the question of how distance in representation space and relatedness in concept space could be connected. The critical assumptions and predictions of the theory are validated on text embeddings and token activations of large language models.

papers.title: Analytical and numerical study of internal representations in multilayer neural networks with binary weights
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the weight space structure of multilayer neural networks with binary weights, focusing on the distribution of volumes associated with internal representations of learning examples. It also analyzes the learning behavior and symmetry breaking transition in such networks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies the internal representation volumes approach to multilayer neural networks with binary weights, deriving the distribution of volumes and analyzing learning behavior and symmetry breaking transitions, with numerical validation.
papers.conclusion: The internal representation volumes approach is confirmed by numerical simulations for binary weight networks, revealing differences from continuous weight networks in where symmetry breaking occurs.
papers.key_findings:
The distribution of internal representation volumes for the binary parity machine can be computed analytically, revealing a freezing transition at α=0.41.
The number of implementable internal representations NR and the number of domains contributing to the Gardner volume ND are derived as functions of the loading parameter α.
The analytical predictions show remarkable agreement with numerical simulations on finite systems.
Multilayer networks with binary weights exhibit symmetry breaking inside representation volumes, unlike continuous weights where it occurs between volumes.
The method provides a detailed geometrical interpretation of the learning transition and the freezing phenomena.
future_direction: Study of the distribution of metastable states arising from a gradient learning process.
papers.abstract: We study the weight space structure of the parity machine with binary weights by deriving the distribution of volumes associated to the internal representations of the learning examples. The learning behavior and the symmetry breaking transition are analyzed and the results are found to be in very good agreement with the extended numerical simulations. \textcopyright{} 1996 The American Physical Society.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Ecco: An Open Source Library for the Explainability of Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the level of syntactic information in BERT's FFNN representations compared to hidden states, and how does syntactic information evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Ecco, an open-source library for explainability of Transformer language models, and uses it to find that syntactic information in BERT's FFNN representations is comparable to hidden states, and that hidden states build up syntactic information even when intermediate FFNNs show diminished levels.
papers.conclusion: Ecco is a tool that aids in debugging, explaining, and building intuitions about Transformer language models, and it is open-source for community contribution.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic information can be retrieved from BERT's FFNN representations at levels comparable to hidden state representations.
The model builds up syntactic information in its hidden states even when intermediate FFNNs indicate diminished levels of syntactic information.
Ecco provides tools for input saliency (gradient-based feature attribution), hidden state evolution analysis, and neuron activation analysis via dimensionality reduction and probing.
The library supports multiple explainability methods (e.g., CCA, NMF, probing) and models (GPT2, BERT, RoBERTa).
Ecco enables interactive exploration of model internals within Jupyter notebooks.
papers.limitation:
Ecco's input saliency feature is currently only supported for GPT2-based models, while neuron activation collection and dimensionality reduction are supported for GPT2, BERT, and RoBERTa.
Visualization is a starting point for building testable and falsifiable hypotheses of model interpretability, not a definitive explanation.
future_direction: Support for more models and explainability methods is under development and open for community contribution.
Future work can examine if the divergence in PoS information between FFNN and hidden states points towards layers storing different subsets of PoS information which the model assembles across layers.
papers.abstract: J Alammar. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations. 2021.

papers.title: Neural Feature Geometry Evolves as Discrete Ricci Flow
papers.research_question: How does the geometry of feature representations evolve in deep neural networks, and does it follow curvature-driven dynamics analogous to discrete Ricci flow?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the evolution of feature geometry in deep neural networks follows curvature-driven dynamics analogous to discrete Ricci flow, and introduces a framework for locally evaluating these transformations, leading to practical design principles like an early-stopping heuristic and depth selection criterion.
papers.conclusion: The evolution of neural feature geometry resembles discrete Ricci flow, and the introduced framework offers practical tools for improving training efficiency and parameter selection.
papers.key_findings:
Deep linear networks preserve feature geometry, while non-linear activations such as ReLU enable meaningful geometric transformations.
The emergence of class separability corresponds to the emergence of community structure in the associated graph representations.
Neural networks consistently impose curvature-driven transformations closely aligned with discrete Ricci flow dynamics across datasets and architectures.
A novel early-stopping heuristic leverages the emergence of curvature-driven geometric behavior during training.
A geometric criterion for network depth selection identifies a critical point beyond which additional layers cease to yield meaningful curvature-driven changes.
papers.limitation:
Computing exact Ollivier-Ricci curvature is computationally demanding.
The curvature gap does not reliably capture how well the graph geometry aligns with the prescribed community structure in the presence of misclassified nodes.
future_direction: Investigate the double descent phenomenon through the lens of local Ricci evolution coefficients.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks learn feature representations via complex geometric transformations of the input data manifold. Despite the models' empirical success across domains, our understanding of neural feature representations is still incomplete. In this work we investigate neural feature geometry through the lens of discrete geometry. Since the input data manifold is typically unobserved, we approximate it using geometric graphs that encode local similarity structure. We provide theoretical results on the evolution of these graphs during training, showing that nonlinear activations play a crucial role in shaping feature geometry in feedforward neural networks. Moreover, we discover that the geometric transformations resemble a discrete Ricci flow on these graphs, suggesting that neural feature geometry evolves analogous to Ricci flow. This connection is supported by experiments on over 20,000 feedforward neural networks trained on binary classification tasks across both synthetic and real-world datasets. We observe that the emergence of class separability corresponds to the emergence of community structure in the associated graph representations, which is known to relate to discrete Ricci flow dynamics. Building on these insights, we introduce a novel framework for locally evaluating geometric transformations through comparison with discrete Ricci flow dynamics. Our results suggest practical design principles, including a geometry-informed early-stopping heuristic and a criterion for selecting network depth.

papers.title: Investigating Network Parameters in Neural-Network Quantum States
papers.research_question: What do the optimized neural-network parameters reveal about the quantum phase transition in the 1D transverse-field Ising model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the quantum phase transition in the 1D transverse-field Ising model is reflected in the optimized RBM parameters, with a qualitative change in the long-range tail of the couplings, leading to a change in the finite-temperature phase diagram of the classical RBM Ising system.
papers.conclusion: The correspondence between neural-network parameters and quantum phases suggests that careful investigation of neural-network parameters may offer a new route to extracting physical insights from neural-network wave functions.
papers.key_findings:
The optimized RBM coupling parameters exhibit long-range behavior in the ordered phase (Γ<1) and short-range behavior in the disordered phase (Γ>1).
The quantum phase transition at Γ=1 is marked by a sharp change in the tail of the RBM coupling parameters.
The finite-temperature specific heat of the RBM Ising system shows a phase transition for Γ<1 but only a crossover for Γ>1.
The energy variance of the RBM system changes qualitatively at the quantum critical point.
Analyzing neural-network parameters can provide physical insights into quantum many-body systems.
papers.limitation: The critical behavior of the 1D TFI model at the phase transition cannot be captured in the current RBM setup because the derivative of the energy has a discontinuity.
future_direction: Investigate other neural networks and other quantum-spin Hamiltonians to see how the neural-network parameters behave.
papers.abstract:
Recently, quantum-state representation using artificial neural networks has
started to be recognized as a powerful tool. However, due to the black-box
nature of machine learning, it is difficult to analyze what machine learns or
why it is powerful. Here, by applying one of the simplest neural networks, the
restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM), to the ground-state representation of the
one-dimensional (1D) transverse-field Ising (TFI) model, we make an attempt to
directly analyze the optimized network parameters. In the RBM optimization, a
zero-temperature quantum state is mapped onto a finite-temperature classical
state of the extended Ising spins that constitute the RBM. We find that the
quantum phase transition from the ordered phase to the disordered phase in the
1D TFI model by increasing the transverse field is clearly reflected in the
behaviors of the optimized RBM parameters and hence in the finite-temperature
phase diagram of the classical RBM Ising system. The present finding of a
correspondence between the neural-network parameters and quantum phases
suggests that a careful investigation of the neural-network parameters may
provide a new route to extracting nontrivial physical insights from the
neural-network wave functions.

papers.title: Data-driven effective model shows a liquid-like deep learning
papers.research_question: What is the geometric structure of the optimization landscape for deep neural networks with binary weights, and how does it differ between deep and shallow networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a statistical mechanics framework that models the weight space of deep binary neural networks, revealing a smooth, connected landscape with a liquid-like core, unlike shallow networks which have a broken weight space.
papers.conclusion: The data-driven effective model provides insights into the high-dimensional weight space of deep learning, showing that deep networks have a smooth, connected landscape with a liquid-like core, which may explain their effectiveness and fast training.
papers.key_findings:
The weight space of deep networks is smooth and dominated by a single well-connected component, while shallow networks exhibit a broken weight space with barriers.
Under-parameterization and over-parameterization belong to the same universal class with a smooth landscape for deep networks.
A liquid-like central part (interior) emerges in deep networks, where weights behave randomly, potentially aiding fast learning.
The effective Ising model accurately captures the weight statistics and can inspire algorithmic designs, such as freezing the interior weights.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is restricted to deep networks with binary weights, which may not fully represent continuous weight networks.
The effective model captures only up to pairwise correlations; higher-order correlations are not considered.
future_direction: Explore whether higher-than-second order correlations enhance understanding of the weight space.
Investigate if there is a qualitative change in the geometric structure around the interpolation threshold (double descent phenomenon).
Study the effect of varying model complexity on the weight space structure.
papers.abstract: The geometric structure of an optimization landscape is argued to be fundamentally important to support the success of deep neural network learning. A direct computation of the landscape beyond two layers is hard. Therefore, to capture the global view of the landscape, an interpretable model of the network-parameter (or weight) space must be established. However, the model is lacking so far. Furthermore, it remains unknown what the landscape looks like for deep networks of binary synapses, which plays a key role in robust and energy efficient neuromorphic computation. Here, we propose a statistical mechanics framework by directly building a least structured model of the high-dimensional weight space, considering realistic structured data, stochastic gradient descent training, and the computational depth of neural networks. We also consider whether the number of network parameters outnumbers the number of supplied training data, namely, over- or under-parametrization. Our least structured model reveals that the weight spaces of the under-parametrization and over-parameterization cases belong to the same class, in the sense that these weight spaces are well connected without any hierarchical clustering structure. In contrast, the shallow-network has a broken weight space, characterized by a discontinuous phase transition, thereby clarifying the benefit of depth in deep learning from the angle of high-dimensional geometry. Our effective model also reveals that inside a deep network, there exists a liquid-like central part of the architecture in the sense that the weights in this part behave as randomly as possible, providing algorithmic implications. Our data-driven model thus provides a statistical mechanics insight about why deep learning is unreasonably effective in terms of the high-dimensional weight space, and how deep networks are different from shallow ones.

papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Unification of Symmetries Inside Neural Networks: Transformer, Feedforward and Neural ODE
papers.research_question: How can gauge symmetries from physics be applied to understand parametric redundancies in neural networks, and can the inner workings of neural networks be interpreted through spacetime diffeomorphisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper unifies symmetries in neural networks by interpreting parametric redundancies as gauge symmetries, showing that gauge symmetries in neural ODEs are spacetime diffeomorphisms, and that rescaling symmetries in feedforward networks and transformers correspond to these diffeomorphisms.
papers.conclusion: Gauge symmetries provide a unifying perspective for analyzing various machine learning architectures, bridging machine learning and physics.
papers.key_findings:
Parametric redundancies in neural networks can be interpreted as gauge symmetries in physics.
Gauge symmetries in neural ODEs are mathematically characterized by spacetime diffeomorphisms.
The rescaling symmetry of feedforward neural networks is lifted to spacetime diffeomorphisms in neural ODEs.
Transformers can be viewed as integrated nonlinear neural ODEs, and their gauge symmetries correspond to diffeomorphisms.
Regularizations in neural networks can be understood as gauge fixing conditions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of neural networks, including transformers, remains one of the most challenging puzzles in machine learning. This study introduces a novel approach by applying the principles of gauge symmetries, a key concept in physics, to neural network architectures. By regarding model functions as physical observables, we find that parametric redundancies of various machine learning models can be interpreted as gauge symmetries. We mathematically formulate the parametric redundancies in neural ODEs, and find that their gauge symmetries are given by spacetime diffeomorphisms, which play a fundamental role in Einstein's theory of gravity. Viewing neural ODEs as a continuum version of feedforward neural networks, we show that the parametric redundancies in feedforward neural networks are indeed lifted to diffeomorphisms in neural ODEs. We further extend our analysis to transformer models, finding natural correspondences with neural ODEs and their gauge symmetries. The concept of gauge symmetries sheds light on the complex behavior of deep learning models through physics and provides us with a unifying perspective for analyzing various machine learning architectures.

papers.title: Relative representations enable zero-shot latent space communication
papers.research_question: Given two different learning models trained separately on different data, can we compare their latent embeddings? The paper investigates how to achieve invariance in latent spaces to enable communication between them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces relative representations, which encode data points by their similarity to a fixed set of anchors. This representation is invariant to angle-preserving transformations in the latent space, enabling zero-shot model stitching and comparison of latent spaces across different trainings, architectures, and data modalities.
papers.conclusion: Relative representations provide a practical and effective way to achieve invariance in latent spaces, enabling zero-shot communication between neural network components and facilitating latent space comparison across diverse settings.
papers.key_findings:
Relative representations preserve the angles between embeddings across different models and training runs, making latent spaces comparable.
The similarity between relative representations of two latent spaces is a strong proxy for model performance, correlating with metrics like accuracy.
Models can be trained end-to-end using relative representations without significant performance drops compared to absolute representations.
Zero-shot stitching of encoder and decoder components from different models (e.g., trained with different seeds, architectures, or on different datasets) is possible using relative representations.
Relative representations enable cross-lingual and cross-architecture zero-shot transfer for tasks like text classification and image reconstruction.
future_direction: Exploring other similarity functions to enforce invariances to non-isometric deformations.
Investigating the use of vector quantization algorithms to achieve invariance to bounded distortion.
papers.abstract: Neural networks embed the geometric structure of a data manifold lying in a high-dimensional space into latent representations. Ideally, the distribution of the data points in the latent space should depend only on the task, the data, the loss, and other architecture-specific constraints. However, factors such as the random weights initialization, training hyperparameters, or other sources of randomness in the training phase may induce incoherent latent spaces that hinder any form of reuse. Nevertheless, we empirically observe that, under the same data and modeling choices, the angles between the encodings within distinct latent spaces do not change. In this work, we propose the latent similarity between each sample and a fixed set of anchors as an alternative data representation, demonstrating that it can enforce the desired invariances without any additional training. We show how neural architectures can leverage these relative representations to guarantee, in practice, invariance to latent isometries and rescalings, effectively enabling latent space communication: from zero-shot model stitching to latent space comparison between diverse settings. We extensively validate the generalization capability of our approach on different datasets, spanning various modalities (images, text, graphs), tasks (e.g., classification, reconstruction) and architectures (e.g., CNNs, GCNs, transformers).

papers.title: The emergence of clusters in self-attention dynamics
papers.research_question: What is the geometric structure of learned representations in Transformers, and how do tokens cluster in the self-attention dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that tokens in the self-attention dynamics cluster to limiting objects (like vertices of convex polytopes or hyperplanes) as time goes to infinity, depending on the spectrum of the value matrix V.
papers.conclusion: Self-attention induces clustering of tokens, confirming the empirical observation of leaders in sequences, with the type of clustering depending on the spectrum of V.
papers.key_findings:
For the one-dimensional case (d=1), the self-attention matrix converges to a low-rank Boolean matrix, indicating the emergence of leaders.
When V = I_d, tokens converge to the boundary of a convex polytope, typically to vertices.
When V has a simple positive leading eigenvalue, tokens cluster toward at most three parallel hyperplanes.
When V has a leading eigenvalue with multiplicity, clustering occurs toward a mix of polytopes and subspaces.
The clustering behavior is confirmed by numerical experiments and is consistent with empirical observations in trained Transformers.
papers.limitation: The analysis does not include multiple heads, feed-forward layers, or layer normalization.
future_direction: Studying multi-headed Transformers.
Characterizing optimal weights via optimal control correspondence.
Extending the analysis to include feed-forward layers.
papers.abstract: Viewing Transformers as interacting particle systems, we describe the geometry of learned representations when the weights are not time dependent. We show that particles, representing tokens, tend to cluster toward particular limiting objects as time tends to infinity. Cluster locations are determined by the initial tokens, confirming context-awareness of representations learned by Transformers. Using techniques from dynamical systems and partial differential equations, we show that the type of limiting object that emerges depends on the spectrum of the value matrix. Additionally, in the one-dimensional case we prove that the self-attention matrix converges to a low-rank Boolean matrix. The combination of these results mathematically confirms the empirical observation made by Vaswani et al. [VSP'17] that leaders appear in a sequence of tokens when processed by Transformers.

papers.title: Information Structure in Mappings: An Approach to Learning, Representation, and Generalisation
papers.research_question: How can we describe the structure of representations in neural networks, how does this structure emerge during training, and what kinds of structures enable generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis introduces quantitative methods for identifying systematic structure in mappings between spaces, and leverages them to understand how deep-learning models learn to represent information, what representational structures drive generalisation, and how design decisions condition the structures that emerge. It also introduces a novel, performant approach to estimating the entropy of vector space.
papers.conclusion: The thesis concludes that information structure methods provide insights into how models learn and generalize, drawing parallels between neural networks and human language.
papers.key_findings:
The methods can identify systematic structure in mappings and relate it to generalization.
There are distinct phases of training: early learning of lexical information followed by contextualization.
Model size affects representational structure: larger models develop more robust representations.
Information structure measures can predict downstream performance.
Regularity in representations is important for generalization.
papers.limitation: It’s unclear if the learnability of a language at timestep n matters at n+1 when the language has changed.
future_direction: Further study of the role learnability plays in an emergent context, where what is learned changes, is needed to understand the full picture.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable success of large large-scale neural networks, we still lack unified notation for thinking about and describing their representational spaces. We lack methods to reliably describe how their representations are structured, how that structure emerges over training, and what kinds of structures are desirable. This thesis introduces quantitative methods for identifying systematic structure in a mapping between spaces, and leverages them to understand how deep-learning models learn to represent information, what representational structures drive generalisation, and how design decisions condition the structures that emerge. To do this I identify structural primitives present in a mapping, along with information theoretic quantifications of each. These allow us to analyse learning, structure, and generalisation across multi-agent reinforcement learning models, sequence-to-sequence models trained on a single task, and Large Language Models. I also introduce a novel, performant, approach to estimating the entropy of vector space, that allows this analysis to be applied to models ranging in size from 1 million to 12 billion parameters. The experiments here work to shed light on how large-scale distributed models of cognition learn, while allowing us to draw parallels between those systems and their human analogs. They show how the structures of language and the constraints that give rise to them in many ways parallel the kinds of structures that drive performance of contemporary neural networks.

papers.title: Closed-Form Interpretation of Neural Network Latent Spaces with Symbolic Gradients
papers.research_question: How can we extract closed-form symbolic interpretations of neurons in neural network latent spaces without prior knowledge of the concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for closed-form interpretation of neurons in neural network latent spaces by matching normalized gradients with symbolic expressions.
papers.conclusion: Developed a framework to interpret any single neuron in neural network latent spaces as a symbolic equation, enabling scientific discovery from latent space models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully retrieves ground truth symbolic expressions for matrix invariants and conserved quantities from Siamese network latent neurons.
The method outperforms direct symbolic regression when the latent encoding is non-linear.
The symbolic search sometimes finds approximate expressions that are mathematically equivalent or Taylor expansions of the ground truth.
The framework is the first general method for extracting concepts from latent spaces in closed form.
papers.limitation: The approach is limited by the expressibility of symbolic search algorithms and the challenge of isolating single neurons through bottlenecks or disentanglement.
papers.abstract: It has been demonstrated that artificial neural networks like autoencoders or Siamese networks encode meaningful concepts in their latent spaces. However, there does not exist a comprehensive framework for retrieving this information in a human-readable form without prior knowledge. In quantitative disciplines concepts are typically formulated as equations. Hence, in order to extract these concepts, we introduce a framework for finding closed-form interpretations of neurons in latent spaces of artificial neural networks. The interpretation framework is based on embedding trained neural networks into an equivalence class of functions that encode the same concept. We interpret these neural networks by finding an intersection between the equivalence class and human-readable equations defined by a symbolic search space. Computationally, this framework is based on finding a symbolic expression whose normalized gradients match the normalized gradients of a specific neuron with respect to the input variables. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated by retrieving invariants of matrices and conserved quantities of dynamical systems from latent spaces of Siamese neural networks.

papers.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories
papers.research_question: What is the function of feed-forward layers in transformer-based language models? The paper shows they operate as key-value memories.
papers.core_contribution: Feed-forward layers in transformer language models function as key-value memories, where keys capture input patterns and values represent output distributions, and the model's final output is constructed by composing and refining these memories across layers.
papers.conclusion: Feed-forward layers in transformers act as pattern-detecting key-value memories, and the model's output is gradually constructed by composing these memories within layers and refining them across layers via residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Keys in feed-forward layers correlate with human-interpretable input patterns, with lower layers capturing shallow patterns (e.g., n-grams) and upper layers capturing semantic patterns.
Values in upper layers induce distributions over the output vocabulary that correlate with the next-token distribution of the patterns in the corresponding keys.
The output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of hundreds of active memories, rarely dominated by a single memory cell.
Residual connections act as a refinement mechanism, with the feed-forward layer often vetoing the residual's top prediction to shift probability mass to other candidates.
The model's final prediction is often determined in the lower layers, with upper layers refining the confidence and occasionally changing the prediction.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to one language model and dataset, and the assumption that all layers operate in the same embedding space may not hold for lower layers.
future_direction: Investigating the transformation of embedding spaces across layers and the interplay between feed-forward and self-attention layers.
Extending the analysis to other transformer models, such as BERT encoders and neural translation models.
Exploring practical implications for interpretability methods, data privacy (e.g., membership inference), and architectural innovations.
papers.abstract: Feed-forward layers constitute two-thirds of a transformer model's parameters, yet their role in the network remains under-explored. We show that feed-forward layers in transformerbased language models operate as key-value memories, where each key correlates with textual patterns in the training examples, and each value induces a distribution over the output vocabulary. Our experiments show that the learned patterns are human-interpretable, and that lower layers tend to capture shallow patterns, while upper layers learn more semantic ones. The values complement the keys' input patterns by inducing output distributions that concentrate probability mass on tokens likely to appear immediately after each pattern, particularly in the upper layers. Finally, we demonstrate that the output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of its memories, which is subsequently refined throughout the model's layers via residual connections to produce the final output distribution.

papers.title: Interpretable statistical representations of neural population dynamics and geometry
papers.research_question: How can we learn interpretable and consistent latent representations of neural population dynamics that evolve on low-dimensional manifolds, and how can we compare these dynamics across conditions, networks, and animals?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MARBLE, an unsupervised geometric deep learning method that learns interpretable latent representations of neural population dynamics by decomposing them into local flow fields, enabling consistent comparison of dynamics across networks and animals.
papers.conclusion: Our results suggest that manifold structure provides a powerful inductive bias to develop powerful decoding algorithms and assimilate data across experiments.
papers.key_findings:
MARBLE discovers low-dimensional latent representations that parametrize high-dimensional neural dynamics during gain modulation, decision-making, and changes in internal state.
MARBLE representations are consistent across neural networks and animals, enabling robust comparison of cognitive computations.
MARBLE outperforms current representation learning approaches (CEBRA, LFADS) in within- and across-animal decoding accuracy.
MARBLE can detect dynamical events such as bifurcations in RNNs corresponding to loss of task performance.
MARBLE can reveal the global geometric structure of latent states (e.g., circular arrangement for reaching directions) without behavioral supervision.
papers.abstract: The dynamics of neuron populations commonly evolve on low-dimensional manifolds. Thus, we need methods that learn the dynamical processes over neural manifolds to infer interpretable and consistent latent representations. We introduce a representation learning method, MARBLE, that decomposes on-manifold dynamics into local flow fields and maps them into a common latent space using unsupervised geometric deep learning. In simulated non-linear dynamical systems, recurrent neural networks, and experimental single-neuron recordings from primates and rodents, we discover emergent low-dimensional latent representations that parametrise high-dimensional neural dynamics during gain modulation, decision-making, and changes in the internal state. These representations are consistent across neural networks and animals, enabling the robust comparison of cognitive computations. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates state-of-the-art within- and across-animal decoding accuracy of MARBLE compared with current representation learning approaches, with minimal user input. Our results suggest that manifold structure provides a powerful inductive bias to develop powerful decoding algorithms and assimilate data across experiments.

papers.title: The algebra and the geometry aspect of Deep learning
papers.research_question: What are the mathematical foundations of deep learning from the perspectives of geometry, algebra, and differential calculus?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a coordinate-free formulation of backpropagation using the canonical scalar product on matrix spaces and explores the geometric and algebraic foundations of deep learning, including connections to algebraic geometry and category theory.
papers.key_findings:
The canonical scalar product on matrix spaces leads to a coordinate-free formulation of backpropagation.
Neural networks can be viewed as approximating separating algebraic varieties, with the degree of the variety related to generalization.
Graph neural networks can be understood through category theory, with cycles in computational graphs related to memory capacity.
The universal approximation theorem is proven using the Hahn-Banach theorem and Riesz representation.
Backpropagation equations are derived using matrix calculus and the chain rule.
future_direction: Development of a mathematical language model trained on propositions and theorems to solve mathematical problems.
Using algebraic geometry to find low-degree separating manifolds for more efficient classification.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the foundations of deep learning through insight of geometry, algebra and differential calculus. At is core, artificial intelligence relies on assumption that data and its intrinsic structure can be embedded into vector spaces allowing for analysis through geometric and algebraic methods. We thrace the development of neural networks from the perceptron to the transformer architecture, emphasizing on the underlying geometric structures and differential processes that govern their behavior. Our original approach highlights how the canonical scalar product on matrix spaces naturally leads to backpropagation equations yielding to a coordinate free formulation. We explore how classification problems can reinterpreted using tools from differential and algebraic geometry suggesting that manifold structure, degree of variety, homology may inform both convergence and interpretability of learning algorithms We further examine how neural networks can be interpreted via their associated directed graph, drawing connection to a Quillen model defined in [1] and [13] to describe memory as an homotopy theoretic property of the associated network.

papers.title: Relative Geometry of Neural Forecasters: Linking Accuracy and Alignment in Learned Latent Geometry
papers.research_question: How do neural forecasters internally represent dynamical systems, and does the alignment of their latent geometries across model families correlate with forecasting accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces anchor-based relative embeddings to compare latent spaces of neural forecasters, revealing family-level alignment patterns and showing that alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy but high accuracy can coexist with low alignment (especially in transformers and ESNs).
papers.conclusion: Relative geometry provides a reproducible foundation for comparing how model families internalize dynamical structure, and alignment offers insights beyond task loss.
papers.key_findings:
Anchor-based relative embeddings remove rotational and scaling ambiguities, enabling direct comparison of latent spaces across model families.
MLPs align with other MLPs, RNNs with RNNs, while transformers and ESNs achieve strong forecasts despite weaker alignment.
Alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy, but high accuracy can coexist with low alignment (especially in transformers and ESNs).
The alignment signal stabilizes with increasing number of anchors (K>=16).
Noise and input length affect representational stability differently across forecasters.
papers.limitation: Alignment with the 'true system' refers only to alignment with the relative representation of observed trajectories, not to recovery of governing equations or physical state variables.
future_direction: Developing bridging mappings between model families
Alignment-driven training interventions
papers.abstract: Neural networks can accurately forecast complex dynamical systems, yet how they internally represent underlying latent geometry remains poorly understood. We study neural forecasters through the lens of representational alignment, introducing anchor-based, geometry-agnostic relative embeddings that remove rotational and scaling ambiguities in latent spaces. Applying this framework across seven canonical dynamical systems - ranging from periodic to chaotic - we reveal reproducible family-level structure: multilayer perceptrons align with other MLPs, recurrent networks with RNNs, while transformers and echo-state networks achieve strong forecasts despite weaker alignment. Alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy, yet high accuracy can coexist with low alignment. Relative geometry thus provides a simple, reproducible foundation for comparing how model families internalize and represent dynamical structure.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
