BERT learns novel concepts (e.g., animal categories, demographic groups) that do not strictly adhere to pre-defined linguistic categories.
Many latent concepts are based on multiple properties (e.g., semantics, syntax, morphology).
Lower layers dominate in learning shallow lexical concepts, while higher layers learn semantic relations.
The discovered latent concepts highlight potential biases learned in the model (e.g., gender and demographic associations).
Concepts learned at higher layers are more aligned with linguistically motivated concepts compared to lower layers.
papers.limitation:
The diversity of observed concepts is limited by the dataset and clustering constraints (memory and algorithm).
Only the final layer of BERT was manually annotated due to annotation cost.
The method is limited to word-level concepts; phrase-level concepts are not explored.
future_direction: Increase diversity of concepts by working around memory and algorithm constraints.
Explore phrase-level concepts.
Incorporate principal component analysis for more controlled analysis.
papers.abstract: A large number of studies that analyze deep neural network models and their ability to encode various linguistic and non-linguistic concepts provide an interpretation of the inner mechanics of these models. The scope of the analyses is limited to pre-defined concepts that reinforce the traditional linguistic knowledge and do not reflect on how novel concepts are learned by the model. We address this limitation by discovering and analyzing latent concepts learned in neural network models in an unsupervised fashion and provide interpretations from the model's perspective. In this work, we study: i) what latent concepts exist in the pre-trained BERT model, ii) how the discovered latent concepts align or diverge from classical linguistic hierarchy and iii) how the latent concepts evolve across layers. Our findings show: i) a model learns novel concepts (e.g. animal categories and demographic groups), which do not strictly adhere to any pre-defined categorization (e.g. POS, semantic tags), ii) several latent concepts are based on multiple properties which may include semantics, syntax, and morphology, iii) the lower layers in the model dominate in learning shallow lexical concepts while the higher layers learn semantic relations and iv) the discovered latent concepts highlight potential biases learned in the model. We also release a novel BERT ConceptNet dataset (BCN) consisting of 174 concept labels and 1M annotated instances.

papers.title: From Information to Generative Exponent: Learning Rate Induces Phase Transitions in SGD
papers.research_question: Can we characterize the regimes of complexity emerging from the choice of learning rate?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that learning rate induces phase transitions in sample complexity, shifting from an information exponent regime to a generative exponent regime, and introduces a new layer-wise training algorithm (alternating SGD) that can achieve linear sample complexity for certain targets.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that algorithms combining correlational and non-correlational update terms exhibit a phase transition in sample complexity regimes as a function of the scaling of the non-correlational term, governed by learning rate.
papers.key_findings:
There is a phase transition in sample complexity as a function of learning rate for gradient-based algorithms learning single-index models.
For batch reuse SGD, the sample complexity interpolates between the information exponent regime and the generative exponent regime depending on the learning rate.
Alternating SGD, a novel layer-wise training algorithm, can achieve linear sample complexity (up to polylog factors) when the square of the link function has information exponent 1 or 2 and the second-layer learning rate is sufficiently large.
The framework captures online SGD, batch reuse SGD, and alternating SGD, showing that the choice of learning rate is as critical as algorithm design for statistical and computational efficiency.
Phase transitions are characterized by thresholds in learning rate that depend on the information and generative exponents of the target link function.
future_direction: Extension of the framework to multi-index models
More general input distributions
Non-polynomial activation functions
Non-constant learning rates
papers.abstract: To understand feature learning dynamics in neural networks, recent theoretical works have focused on gradient-based learning of Gaussian single-index models, where the label is a nonlinear function of a latent one-dimensional projection of the input. While the sample complexity of online SGD is determined by the information exponent of the link function, recent works improved this by performing multiple gradient steps on the same sample with different learning rates -- yielding a non-correlational update rule -- and instead are limited by the (potentially much smaller) generative exponent. However, this picture is only valid when these learning rates are sufficiently large. In this paper, we characterize the relationship between learning rate(s) and sample complexity for a broad class of gradient-based algorithms that encapsulates both correlational and non-correlational updates. We demonstrate that, in certain cases, there is a phase transition from an "information exponent regime" with small learning rate to a "generative exponent regime" with large learning rate. Our framework covers prior analyses of one-pass SGD and SGD with batch reuse, while also introducing a new layer-wise training algorithm that leverages a two-timescales approach (via different learning rates for each layer) to go beyond correlational queries without reusing samples or modifying the loss from squared error. Our theoretical study demonstrates that the choice of learning rate is as important as the design of the algorithm in achieving statistical and computational efficiency.

papers.title: Intrinsic dimension of data representations in deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How does the intrinsic dimension of data representations change across layers of convolutional neural networks, and how is it related to generalization performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in trained deep neural networks, the intrinsic dimension of data representations is much smaller than the embedding dimension, follows a characteristic 'hunchback' shape across layers (first increasing then decreasing), and the ID in the last hidden layer predicts generalization performance.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks that generalize well transform data into low-dimensional, curved manifolds, and the progressive reduction of intrinsic dimension across layers is a key signature of generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimension (ID) of data representations in deep neural networks is orders of magnitude smaller than the number of units in each layer.
Across layers, the ID first increases and then progressively decreases, forming a 'hunchback' shape.
The ID of the last hidden layer predicts classification accuracy on the test set, with lower ID correlating with better generalization.
These properties are not found in untrained networks or networks trained on randomized labels, indicating they are linked to generalization.
Data representations lie on curved manifolds, as linear dimensionality estimates (e.g., PCA) give much higher values than the ID.
papers.limitation:
For intrinsic dimension larger than ~20 and finite sample size, the TwoNN estimator moderately underestimates the correct value.
The analysis is limited to convolutional neural networks for image classification.
The dynamics of ID during training may depend on the specific architecture and dataset, and is not strictly monotonic.
future_direction: Further investigation into the dynamics of ID during training across different architectures and datasets.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks progressively transform their inputs across multiple processing layers. What are the geometrical properties of the representations learned by these networks? Here we study the intrinsic dimensionality (ID) of data-representations, i.e. the minimal number of parameters needed to describe a representation. We find that, in a trained network, the ID is orders of magnitude smaller than the number of units in each layer. Across layers, the ID first increases and then progressively decreases in the final layers. Remarkably, the ID of the last hidden layer predicts classification accuracy on the test set. These results can neither be found by linear dimensionality estimates (e.g., with principal component analysis), nor in representations that had been artificially linearized. They are neither found in untrained networks, nor in networks that are trained on randomized labels. This suggests that neural networks that can generalize are those that transform the data into low-dimensional, but not necessarily flat manifolds.

papers.title: Triple Phase Transitions: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Large Language Models from a Neuroscience Perspective
papers.research_question: How do phase transitions in large language model training manifest in terms of alignment with human brain activity, internal representations, and downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three common phase transitions in LLM training: an initial alignment with the brain when instruction following emerges, a detachment during task performance stagnation, and a realignment when tasks are consolidated.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM learning involves three phase transitions that synchronize brain alignment, internal representations, and task performance, providing a multi-scale view of emergent abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Phase 1 (Brain Alignment and Instruction Following): Alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions.
Phase 2 (Brain Detachment and Stagnation): LLMs diverge from the brain during a period of downstream task accuracy stagnation.
Phase 3 (Brain Realignment and Consolidation): Alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving downstream tasks.
These three phase transitions are observed across LLMs with distinct architectures and training data.
The transitions only occur when the input language matches a language sufficiently represented in the model's training corpus.
papers.limitation: The brain encoding accuracy and intrinsic dimensionality are not perfectly congruent, leaving open questions about what aspects of activation changes are not captured by intrinsic dimensionality alone.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit abrupt emergent behavior, whereby new abilities arise at certain points during their training. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as a ''phase transition'', remains poorly understood. In this study, we conduct an integrative analysis of such phase transitions by examining three interconnected perspectives: the similarity between LLMs and the human brain, the internal states of LLMs, and downstream task performance. We propose a novel interpretation for the learning dynamics of LLMs that vary in both training data and architecture, revealing that three phase transitions commonly emerge across these models during training: (1) alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions Brain Alignment and Instruction Following, (2) unexpectedly, LLMs diverge from the brain during a period in which downstream task accuracy temporarily stagnates Brain Detachment and Stagnation, and (3) alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving the downstream tasks Brain Realignment and Consolidation. These findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions in LLMs, while opening new avenues for interdisciplinary research bridging AI and neuroscience.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: The Bottom-up Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: A Study with Machine Translation and Language Modeling Objectives
papers.research_question: How do the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in Transformers under different learning objectives (machine translation, language modeling, masked language modeling)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes viewing token representation evolution in Transformers through a compression/prediction trade-off, and shows through experiments that different objectives (MT, LM, MLM) lead to distinct patterns of information flow, with MLM exhibiting a two-stage process of context encoding and token reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: The learning objective determines the information flow in the model, and the proposed compression/prediction perspective helps explain the behavior and relates findings to prior probing task results, suggesting MLM may be superior for pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
For LM, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past gets lost and predictions about the future get formed.
For MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity and producing a more generalized token representation; the token identity then gets recreated at the top layer.
For MT, though representations get refined with context, less processing is happening and most information about the word type does not get lost.
Differences due to training objective are much larger than those due to random initialization.
Frequent tokens change more than rare ones in all layers for LM and MT, but for MLM the pattern is different with two stages; rare tokens generally influence more than frequent ones, except in MLM where the model learns not to over-rely on rare tokens before context is understood.
papers.limitation: Direct mutual information estimation from finite samples for densities on multi-dimensional spaces is challenging.
papers.abstract: We seek to understand how the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in deep neural networks under different learning objectives. We focus on the Transformers for our analysis as they have been shown effective on various tasks, including machine translation (MT), standard left-to-right language models (LM) and masked language modeling (MLM). Previous work used black-box probing tasks to show that the representations learned by the Transformer differ significantly depending on the objective. In this work, we use canonical correlation analysis and mutual information estimators to study how information flows across Transformer layers and how this process depends on the choice of learning objective. For example, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past in left-to-right language models gets vanished and predictions about the future get formed. In contrast, for MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity and producing a more generalized token representation. The token identity then gets recreated at the top MLM layers.

papers.title: Black Boxes and Looking Glasses: Multilevel Symmetries, Reflection Planes, and Convex Optimization in Deep Networks
papers.research_question: Is there a fundamental difference in the nature of functions learned by deep networks, as opposed to shallow networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that training deep narrow networks with absolute value activation is equivalent to convex Lasso problems, revealing that deep networks learn multilevel symmetries via reflections of training data.
papers.conclusion: The paper proves an equivalence between neural networks and Lasso problems with novel geometric features, and suggests that multi-level symmetries may hold for standard ReLU networks as future work.
papers.key_findings:
Training deep neural networks with absolute value activation can be formulated as equivalent convex Lasso problems.
Deep networks favor symmetric structures, with greater depth enabling multilevel symmetries (symmetries within symmetries).
The Lasso features represent distances to reflection hyperplanes that are spanned by training data and orthogonal to optimal weight vectors.
For 3-layer networks, explicit Lasso dictionaries are given and the optimal first-layer weight is orthogonal to a subset of augmented training data.
Neural networks trained using LLM embeddings learn reflection features similar to those predicted by the Lasso model.
papers.limitation: The choice of absolute value activation and ℓ1 regularization is needed for analytic tractability, which may limit direct applicability to standard ReLU networks.
future_direction: Extensions to ReLU networks.
Analysis of Lasso solution sets and stationary points for higher dimensional data.
Investigation of reflection features in wider ReLU architectures with higher-dimensional data.
papers.abstract: We show that training deep neural networks (DNNs) with absolute value activation and arbitrary input dimension can be formulated as equivalent convex Lasso problems with novel features expressed using geometric algebra. This formulation reveals geometric structures encoding symmetry in neural networks. Using the equivalent Lasso form of DNNs, we formally prove a fundamental distinction between deep and shallow networks: deep networks inherently favor symmetric structures in their fitted functions, with greater depth enabling multilevel symmetries, i.e., symmetries within symmetries. Moreover, Lasso features represent distances to hyperplanes that are reflected across training points. These reflection hyperplanes are spanned by training data and are orthogonal to optimal weight vectors. Numerical experiments support theory and demonstrate theoretically predicted features when training networks using embeddings generated by Large Language Models.

papers.title: Visualizing LLM Latent Space Geometry Through Dimensionality Reduction
papers.research_question: How does the internal geometric structure of latent states in Transformer-based language models evolve across layers and components?
papers.core_contribution: This paper visualizes and analyzes the latent space geometry of Transformer-based LLMs, revealing a clear geometric separation between attention and MLP component outputs, characterizing high-norm latent states at initial sequence positions, and visualizing layerwise evolution and positional effects.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how dimensionality reduction can reveal geometric patterns in LLM latent spaces, contributing to interpretability research and motivating further analysis of feature geometry across models and conditions.
papers.key_findings:
A clear geometric separation exists between the outputs of attention and MLP components in intermediate layers, a pattern not previously documented.
Latent states at the initial sequence position have high norms, extending beyond special tokens in LLaMa despite its use of relative positional encodings.
Layerwise norms of latent states (excluding initial tokens) gradually increase and then spike in the final block before dropping after the final normalization.
GPT-2's learned positional embeddings form a high-dimensional helical structure in latent space.
LLaMa's sequence-position-dependent latent states show a low-dimensional geometric pattern, though the cause (RoPE vs. other factors) remains unclear.
papers.limitation: For LLaMa, the visualizations alone cannot determine whether the observed geometric patterns are due to RoPE, the convergence of features from self-attention heads, or both.
future_direction: Further understanding the dynamics of latent states across layers, models, and experimental conditions.
Interpreting the sequence-wise latent state geometric patterns of models using Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE).
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art results across many natural language tasks, but their internal mechanisms remain difficult to interpret. In this work, we extract, process, and visualize latent state geometries in Transformer-based language models through dimensionality reduction. We capture layerwise activations at multiple points within Transformer blocks and enable systematic analysis through Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). We demonstrate experiments on GPT-2 and LLaMa models, where we uncover interesting geometric patterns in latent space. Notably, we identify a clear separation between attention and MLP component outputs across intermediate layers, a pattern not documented in prior work to our knowledge. We also characterize the high norm of latent states at the initial sequence position and visualize the layerwise evolution of latent states. Additionally, we demonstrate the high-dimensional helical structure of GPT-2's positional embeddings and the sequence-wise geometric patterns in LLaMa. We make our code available at https://github.com/Vainateya/Feature_Geometry_Visualization.

papers.title: Spring-block theory of feature learning in deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How does feature learning in deep neural networks emerge from the interplay of nonlinearity, noise, learning rate, and other factors, and can it be explained by a macroscopic mechanical theory?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a spring-block mechanical theory that explains the noise-nonlinearity phase diagram of feature learning in deep neural networks and connects layerwise data separation to generalization.
papers.conclusion: The spring-block model provides a top-down phenomenological explanation for feature learning in DNNs, linking noise and nonlinearity to layerwise data separation and generalization, with implications for hyperparameter tuning.
papers.key_findings:
DNN training shows a noise-nonlinearity phase diagram where concave load curves (deep layers learn better) occur with high nonlinearity and low noise, while convex curves (shallow layers learn better) occur with high noise and low nonlinearity.
A spring-block chain model with asymmetric friction captures the dynamics of data separation across layers, explaining the phase diagram.
Noise in training (from dropout, batch size, etc.) rebalances the load across layers, reducing effective friction and leading to more uniform separation.
Nonlinearity acts like friction, absorbing load and causing deeper layers to separate data more, leading to concave load curves.
Linear load curves (equiseparation) are associated with the highest test accuracy, suggesting a link between balanced feature learning and generalization.
papers.limitation: The theory applies only to DNNs with homogeneous layers; heterogeneous architectures require new models.
future_direction: Extending the theory to heterogeneous DNNs with different layer types.
Developing new hyperparameter tuning and model selection strategies based on the spring-block analogy.
papers.abstract: Feature-learning deep nets progressively collapse data to a regular low-dimensional geometry. How this emerges from the collective action of nonlinearity, noise, learning rate, and other factors, has eluded first-principles theories built from microscopic neuronal dynamics. We exhibit a noise-nonlinearity phase diagram that identifies regimes where shallow or deep layers learn more effectively and propose a macroscopic mechanical theory that reproduces the diagram and links feature learning across layers to generalization.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Hierarchical Associative Memory, Parallelized MLP-Mixer, and Symmetry Breaking
papers.research_question: How can hierarchical associative memory be integrated with MetaFormers to represent Transformer blocks as Hopfield networks, and what is the impact of symmetry in weight matrices on performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper integrates hierarchical associative memory with MetaFormers to derive a parallelized MLP-Mixer from a three-layer Hopfield network, and shows that symmetry-breaking in weight matrices is crucial for performance in image recognition tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a correspondence between Hopfield networks and MLP-Mixer models, demonstrating that symmetry breaking in weight matrices is essential for effective performance in image recognition.
papers.key_findings:
Symmetric weight matrices in Mixer models hinder performance on image recognition tasks.
Introducing symmetry-breaking effects improves performance to match vanilla MLP-Mixer.
Parallelized MLP-Mixer (ParaMixer) performs competitively with vanilla MLP-Mixer.
Iterative application of mixing layers shows that SymMixer maintains performance over iterations, while ParaMixer degrades.
The degeneracy of attractors in Hopfield networks is resolved by symmetry breaking.
papers.limitation:
narrow focus on the Lagrangians in the formulation
lack of examination of applications to practical problems
future_direction: Reconsideration of Lagrangians for hidden neurons
Exploration of task domains suitable for SymMixer such as denoising or image retrieval
Quantitative analysis of memorization capacity
papers.abstract: Transformers have established themselves as the leading neural network model in natural language processing and are increasingly foundational in various domains. In vision, the MLP-Mixer model has demonstrated competitive performance, suggesting that attention mechanisms might not be indispensable. Inspired by this, recent research has explored replacing attention modules with other mechanisms, including those described by MetaFormers. However, the theoretical framework for these models remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes a novel perspective by integrating Krotov's hierarchical associative memory with MetaFormers, enabling a comprehensive representation of the entire Transformer block, encompassing token-/channel-mixing modules, layer normalization, and skip connections, as a single Hopfield network. This approach yields a parallelized MLP-Mixer derived from a three-layer Hopfield network, which naturally incorporates symmetric token-/channel-mixing modules and layer normalization. Empirical studies reveal that symmetric interaction matrices in the model hinder performance in image recognition tasks. Introducing symmetry-breaking effects transitions the performance of the symmetric parallelized MLP-Mixer to that of the vanilla MLP-Mixer. This indicates that during standard training, weight matrices of the vanilla MLP-Mixer spontaneously acquire a symmetry-breaking configuration, enhancing their effectiveness. These findings offer insights into the intrinsic properties of Transformers and MLP-Mixers and their theoretical underpinnings, providing a robust framework for future model design and optimization.

papers.title: Koopman Autoencoders Learn Neural Representation Dynamics
papers.research_question: Can we discover a dynamics that generates the path of neural representations through network layers? And, when equipped with the dynamics, can we edit these dynamics to produce a different output than what was originally intended?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Koopman autoencoders as a framework for interpolating and editing the neural representations of a trained neural network, with an encoder isometry objective to preserve original topology, enabling targeted class unlearning.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates how Koopman theory can provide a practical framework for working with neural representations, opening new avenues for analyzing deep networks through the lens of dynamical systems.
papers.key_findings:
Koopman autoencoders can interpolate between neural representations, and the intermediate representations they generate naturally simplify in topology, replicating the progressive simplification observed in the original network.
The encoder isometry objective helps preserve the original topology of neural representations in the observable space, making topological edits in observable space reflect in state space.
The method enables targeted class unlearning by editing the linear operator governing the dynamics in observable space, which is particularly effective when the penultimate layer representations exhibit neural collapse (as in MNIST).
The approach provides a way to visualize how data is transformed within a neural network via the learned dynamics and dimensionality reduction.
papers.limitation:
The approach is limited to interpolating between two neural representations (first and penultimate layers).
The method is demonstrated on residual MLPs; extending it to other architectures (e.g., convolutional layers, transformer blocks) is future work.
future_direction: Regularizing the dynamics to interpolate through all the intermediate representations of a model.
Investigating whether spectral analysis of the Koopman operator offers insights into the original model's mechanism.
Exploring other favorable topologies in observable space that enable goals like disentanglement, interpretability, or unlearning.
Extending the framework to different architectures (e.g., transformers) and tasks like concept unlearning in language models.
papers.abstract: This paper explores a simple question: can we model the internal transformations of a neural network using dynamical systems theory? We introduce Koopman autoencoders to capture how neural representations evolve through network layers, treating these representations as states in a dynamical system. Our approach learns a surrogate model that predicts how neural representations transform from input to output, with two key advantages. First, by way of lifting the original states via an autoencoder, it operates in a linear space, making editing the dynamics straightforward. Second, it preserves the topologies of the original representations by regularizing the autoencoding objective. We demonstrate that these surrogate models naturally replicate the progressive topological simplification observed in neural networks. As a practical application, we show how our approach enables targeted class unlearning in the Yin-Yang and MNIST classification tasks.

papers.title: Correlation of internal representations in feed-forward neural networks
papers.research_question: How do correlations between hidden node activities in feed-forward neural networks arise near saturation, and how can they be calculated for arbitrary decoder functions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows how to calculate correlations between hidden node activities in feed-forward neural networks near saturation, and provides explicit formulas for parity, AND, and committee machines.
papers.conclusion: The correlations between hidden nodes in feed-forward neural networks near saturation can be calculated and are determined by the decoder function, and these results are likely robust to replica symmetry breaking.
papers.key_findings:
For the parity-machine, all legal internal representations have equal probability, leading to zero correlations for n<K and cK=1.
For the AND-machine, correlations are dominated by the restrictive output case σ=+1, resulting in cn = 1/2 - n2^{-K}/K.
For the committee-machine, correlations are given by explicit formulas (13) and (14), with specific asymptotic behavior for large K.
The correlations near saturation are determined by the decoder function and the distribution of internal representations.
The results rely on replica symmetry but are likely robust to replica symmetry breaking.
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes replica symmetry, while replica symmetry breaking is known to be crucial for storage capacity calculations.
future_direction: Determine the storage capacity of an ensemble of uncoupled perceptrons with prescribed correlations.
papers.abstract:
Feed-forward multilayer neural networks implementing random input-output
mappings develop characteristic correlations between the activity of their
hidden nodes which are important for the understanding of the storage and
generalization performance of the network. It is shown how these correlations
can be calculated from the joint probability distribution of the aligning
fields at the hidden units for arbitrary decoder function between hidden layer
and output. Explicit results are given for the parity-, and-, and
committee-machines with arbitrary number of hidden nodes near saturation.

papers.title: Phase Diagram of Initial Condensation for Two-Layer Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the dynamical regimes of two-layer neural networks under varying initialization scales, and how does initialization affect condensation?
papers.core_contribution: Establishes a phase diagram for initial condensation in two-layer neural networks, explaining the dependence on hyperparameters and the mechanism by which small initialization leads to condensation.
papers.key_findings:
Condensation of weight vectors occurs during training, leading to better generalization abilities.
The phase diagram illustrates dynamical regimes of neural networks based on initialization scales.
Small initialization leads to condensation at the initial training stage.
papers.abstract: The phenomenon of distinct behaviors exhibited by neural networks under varying scales of initialization remains an enigma in deep learning research.In this paper, based on the earlier work [Luo et al., J. Mach.Learn.Res., 22:1-47, 2021], we present a phase diagram of initial condensation for two-layer neural networks.Condensation is a phenomenon wherein the weight vectors of neural networks concentrate on isolated orientations during the training process, and it is a feature in nonlinear learning process that enables neural networks to possess better generalization abilities.Our phase diagram serves to provide a comprehensive understanding of the dynamical regimes of neural networks and their dependence on the choice of hyperparameters related to initialization.Furthermore, we demonstrate in detail the underlying mechanisms by which small initialization leads to condensation at the initial training stage.

papers.title: What Do Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn?
papers.research_question: What do self-supervised vision transformers learn? Specifically, how and why contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM) differ in their representations and downstream task performance.
papers.core_contribution: CL and MIM learn complementary representations: CL captures global shape information but suffers from attention collapse, while MIM captures local texture information and preserves diversity. A simple linear combination of both losses can outperform each individually.
papers.conclusion: CL and MIM have opposing properties and are complementary; combining them can improve performance, and even a simple harmonization method shows benefits.
papers.key_findings:
CL trains self-attentions to capture global patterns and object shapes, but leads to attention collapse into homogeneity, reducing representation diversity.
MIM focuses on local patterns and textures, preserving token-level diversity and excelling in fine-tuning and dense prediction tasks.
CL utilizes low-frequency signals (shape-biased), while MIM utilizes high-frequency signals (texture-biased).
CL plays a crucial role in later layers, while MIM is important in early layers.
A simple linear combination of CL and MIM objectives can leverage the advantages of both methods, improving performance in linear probing and fine-tuning.
future_direction: Exploring better ways to combine CL and MIM than linear combination, such as applying CL in later layers and MIM in early layers.
Extending findings to multi-stage Vision Transformers like PiT and Swin.
Enhancing individual properties of CL and MIM to improve shape or texture learning.
papers.abstract: We present a comparative study on how and why contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM) differ in their representations and in their performance of downstream tasks. In particular, we demonstrate that self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) have the following properties: (1) CL trains self-attentions to capture longer-range global patterns than MIM, such as the shape of an object, especially in the later layers of the ViT architecture. This CL property helps ViTs linearly separate images in their representation spaces. However, it also makes the self-attentions collapse into homogeneity for all query tokens and heads. Such homogeneity of self-attention reduces the diversity of representations, worsening scalability and dense prediction performance. (2) CL utilizes the low-frequency signals of the representations, but MIM utilizes high-frequencies. Since low- and high-frequency information respectively represent shapes and textures, CL is more shape-oriented and MIM more texture-oriented. (3) CL plays a crucial role in the later layers, while MIM mainly focuses on the early layers. Upon these analyses, we find that CL and MIM can complement each other and observe that even the simplest harmonization can help leverage the advantages of both methods. The code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/cl-vs-mim.

papers.title: A phase transition between positional and semantic learning in a solvable model of dot-product attention
papers.research_question: What conditions lead to the emergence of positional versus semantic attention mechanisms in a dot-product attention model, and is there a phase transition between these regimes as sample complexity increases?
papers.core_contribution: We provide a tight theoretical analysis of a solvable dot-product attention model, showing a phase transition between positional and semantic learning mechanisms as sample complexity increases, and demonstrate that the attention layer outperforms a linear baseline when learning the semantic mechanism given sufficient data.
papers.conclusion: We have provided a theoretical characterization of the emergence of semantic attention in a dot-product attention model, showing a phase transition between positional and semantic learning regimes, opening the door to further theoretical studies of phase transitions in attention-based models.
papers.key_findings:
The model exhibits two distinct minima: a positional attention mechanism (tokens attend based on position) and a semantic attention mechanism (tokens attend based on meaning).
There exists a phase transition from the positional to the semantic minimum as the sample complexity increases.
The dot-product attention layer outperforms a linear positional baseline when it learns the semantic mechanism, given sufficient data.
The phase transition is sharp and can be characterized analytically in the high-dimensional limit.
The global minimum of the empirical loss landscape switches between positional and semantic solutions at a critical sample complexity, which depends on the task's positional/semantic composition.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a simplified model with a single attention layer, tied low-rank weights, and Gaussian input data.
future_direction: Extensions to more complex architectures and data distributions
Rigorous justification of the GAMP convergence
Study of phase transitions in deeper transformer models
papers.abstract: Many empirical studies have provided evidence for the emergence of algorithmic mechanisms (abilities) in the learning of language models, that lead to qualitative improvements of the model capabilities. Yet, a theoretical characterization of how such mechanisms emerge remains elusive. In this paper, we take a step in this direction by providing a tight theoretical analysis of the emergence of semantic attention in a solvable model of dot-product attention. More precisely, we consider a non-linear self-attention layer with trainable tied and low-rank query and key matrices. In the asymptotic limit of high-dimensional data and a comparably large number of training samples we provide a tight closed-form characterization of the global minimum of the non-convex empirical loss landscape. We show that this minimum corresponds to either a positional attention mechanism (with tokens attending to each other based on their respective positions) or a semantic attention mechanism (with tokens attending to each other based on their meaning), and evidence an emergent phase transition from the former to the latter with increasing sample complexity. Finally, we compare the dot-product attention layer to a linear positional baseline, and show that it outperforms the latter using the semantic mechanism provided it has access to sufficient data.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Feature Identification via the Empirical NTK
papers.research_question: Whether eigenanalysis of the empirical neural tangent kernel (eNTK) can surface the features used by trained neural networks.
papers.core_contribution: Eigenanalysis of the empirical NTK can recover ground-truth features in toy models, localize features to specific layers, and detect grokking phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: eNTK analysis provides a practical handle for feature discovery and for detecting phase changes in small models.
papers.key_findings:
In Toy Models of Superposition, the eNTK recovers ground-truth features in both sparse and dense regimes.
For a 1-layer MLP trained on modular arithmetic, the eNTK recovers Fourier feature families and localizes them to layers; the spectrum develops cliffs that align with the grokking phase transition.
For a 1-layer Transformer trained on modular arithmetic, the eNTK eigendirections align with Fourier features at key frequencies in specific layers.
Layerwise eNTK can localize features to specific layers.
The evolution of the eNTK spectrum can be used to diagnose the grokking phase transition.
papers.limitation:
The empirical NTK hypothesis may not hold in general, and its applicability to realistic models is not established.
Experiments are limited to small toy models; it is unclear if the method scales to large models.
future_direction: Understanding analytically the properties leading to clean signals in the eNTK.
Developing unsupervised feature discovery using eNTK eigendirections.
Applying eNTK analysis to larger models like OthelloGPT and realistic LLMs.
papers.abstract: We provide evidence that eigenanalysis of the empirical neural tangent kernel (eNTK) can surface the features used by trained neural networks. Across three standard toy models for mechanistic interpretability, Toy Models of Superposition (TMS), a 1-layer MLP trained on modular addition and a 1-layer Transformer trained on modular addition, we find that top eigenspaces of the eNTK align with ground-truth features. In TMS, the eNTK recovers the ground-truth features in both the sparse (high superposition) and dense regimes. In modular arithmetic, the eNTK can be used to recover Fourier feature families. Moreover, we provide evidence that a layerwise eNTK localizes features to specific layers and that the evolution of the eNTK spectrum can be used to diagnose the grokking phase transition. These results suggest that eNTK analysis may provide a practical handle for feature discovery and for detecting phase changes in small models.

papers.title: Formation of Representations in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do latent representations, weights, and gradients become aligned during training in neural networks? What universal principles govern the formation of representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Canonical Representation Hypothesis (CRH), which states that representations, weights, and gradients become mutually aligned during training due to noise-regularization balance, and the Polynomial Alignment Hypothesis (PAH), which describes power-law scaling when CRH breaks.
papers.conclusion: The CRH provides a new perspective for studying representation formation in neural networks and unifies several deep learning phenomena, with future work needed to understand the phases of PAH and extend the theory to non-fully-connected layers.
papers.key_findings:
The Canonical Representation Hypothesis (CRH) is proposed and empirically validated across various neural networks.
The balance between gradient noise and regularization is crucial for the emergence of aligned representations.
Breaking of the CRH leads to the Polynomial Alignment Hypothesis (PAH), characterized by reciprocal power-law relations between representations, weights, and gradients.
The CRH generalizes and unifies phenomena such as neural collapse and the neural feature ansatz.
Experiments on fully connected networks, ResNets, and transformers show strong alignment in later layers, with different layers often in different PAH phases.
papers.limitation: The CRH and PAH apply only to fully connected layers, and a future step is extending them to other types of layers.
future_direction: Understand the conditions that lead to each phase of the Polynomial Alignment Hypothesis and how these phases affect model behavior and performance.
Extend the CRH and PAH to non-fully-connected layers, such as convolutional or attention layers.
papers.abstract: Understanding neural representations will help open the black box of neural networks and advance our scientific understanding of modern AI systems. However, how complex, structured, and transferable representations emerge in modern neural networks has remained a mystery. Building on previous results, we propose the Canonical Representation Hypothesis (CRH), which posits a set of six alignment relations to universally govern the formation of representations in most hidden layers of a neural network. Under the CRH, the latent representations (R), weights (W), and neuron gradients (G) become mutually aligned during training. This alignment implies that neural networks naturally learn compact representations, where neurons and weights are invariant to task-irrelevant transformations. We then show that the breaking of CRH leads to the emergence of reciprocal power-law relations between R, W, and G, which we refer to as the Polynomial Alignment Hypothesis (PAH). We present a minimal-assumption theory proving that the balance between gradient noise and regularization is crucial for the emergence of the canonical representation. The CRH and PAH lead to an exciting possibility of unifying major key deep learning phenomena, including neural collapse and the neural feature ansatz, in a single framework.

papers.title: Measuring the Mixing of Contextual Information in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How is contextual information mixed across the Transformer architecture, and how can this mixing be measured to provide faithful explanations for model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALTI, an interpretability method that measures token-to-token interactions within each Transformer layer and aggregates them to provide input attribution scores, demonstrating more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: ALTI is a powerful interpretability method that quantifies the mixing of information in the Transformer, providing faithful input attributions and opening new possibilities for studying contextual information aggregation.
papers.key_findings:
ALTI outperforms gradient-based and other attribution methods in faithfulness metrics (comprehensiveness and sufficiency) across multiple models and datasets.
ALTI provides more robust interpretations across models with identical architecture but different random initializations, as measured by Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation.
Using ℓ1 norm for measuring token contributions in ALTI is beneficial due to the anisotropic nature of Transformer representations and the presence of outlier dimensions.
The proposed layer-wise contribution measurement (based on distance to the output) significantly improves upon a previous norm-based approach.
Including the second layer normalization (from the feed-forward module) in the analysis has negligible impact on the faithfulness of the interpretations.
papers.limitation:
ALTI does not consider the classifier on top of the Transformer and therefore does not provide explanations for each of the output classes, unlike gradient-based methods.
Faithfulness is evaluated only via sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture aggregates input information through the self-attention mechanism, but there is no clear understanding of how this information is mixed across the entire model. Additionally, recent works have demonstrated that attention weights alone are not enough to describe the flow of information. In this paper, we consider the whole attention block --multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization-- and define a metric to measure token-to-token interactions within each layer. Then, we aggregate layer-wise interpretations to provide input attribution scores for model predictions. Experimentally, we show that our method, ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions), provides more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.

papers.title: nDNA -- the Semantic Helix of Artificial Cognition
papers.research_question: How can we characterize and compare the latent semantic genomes of diverse LLMs? What geometric invariants define model ancestry, inheritance, and epistemic divergence?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Neural DNA (nDNA) as a semantic-genotypic representation that captures the latent identity of foundation models through the intrinsic geometry of belief, integrating spectral curvature, thermodynamic length, and belief gradients to form a diagnostic framework for neural genomics.
papers.conclusion: Proposes nDNA and Neural Genomics as a framework for understanding the evolving anatomy of artificial cognition, offering a grammar for diagnosing and governing model lineage, drift, and internal alignment.
papers.abstract: As AI foundation models grow in capability, a deeper question emerges: What shapes their internal cognitive identity -- beyond fluency and output? Benchmarks measure behavior, but the soul of a model resides in its latent geometry. In this work, we propose Neural DNA (nDNA) as a semantic-genotypic representation that captures this latent identity through the intrinsic geometry of belief. At its core, nDNA is synthesized from three principled and indispensable dimensions of latent geometry: spectral curvature, which reveals the curvature of conceptual flow across layers; thermodynamic length, which quantifies the semantic effort required to traverse representational transitions through layers; and belief vector field, which delineates the semantic torsion fields that guide a model's belief directional orientations. Like biological DNA, it encodes ancestry, mutation, and semantic inheritance, found in finetuning and alignment scars, cultural imprints, and architectural drift. In naming it, we open a new field: Neural Genomics, where models are not just tools, but digital semantic organisms with traceable inner cognition. Modeling statement. We read AI foundation models as semantic fluid dynamics: meaning is transported through layers like fluid in a shaped conduit; nDNA is the physics-grade readout of that flow -- a geometry-first measure of how meaning is bent, paid for, and pushed -- yielding a stable, coordinate-free neural DNA fingerprint tied to on-input behavior; with this fingerprint we cross into biology: tracing lineages across pretraining, fine-tuning, alignment, pruning, distillation, and merges; measuring inheritance between checkpoints; detecting drift as traits shift under new data or objectives; and, ultimately, studying the evolution of artificial cognition to compare models, diagnose risks, and govern change over time.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Beyond Signal Propagation: Is Feature Diversity Necessary in Deep Neural\n Network Initialization?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether feature diversity in neural network initialization is necessary for successful training, by constructing networks with identical features at initialization.
papers.core_contribution: Random, diverse initializations are not necessary for training neural networks; networks with identical features at initialization can achieve high accuracy when trained with a symmetry-breaking mechanism, such as non-deterministic GPU operations.
papers.conclusion: Feature diversity is not necessary in neural network initialization, and symmetry breaking is a key factor for training networks with symmetric initializations.
papers.key_findings:
Networks with identical features at initialization (ConstNet) can achieve high accuracy on standard benchmarks when trained with symmetry breaking mechanisms.
Non-deterministic GPU operations can serve as a sufficient source of symmetry breaking to enable training.
Without symmetry breaking, training fails.
The forward and backward weight correlations in ConstNet converge to similar values as in randomly initialized networks.
In shallow networks, feature replication degrades performance, but adding small noise ameliorates this.
papers.limitation:
0-initialized networks are less robust to learning rate changes and may have slower convergence.
Reliance on hardware noise for symmetry breaking may lead to variability across different hardware and insufficient breaking in 16-bit training.
Dropout alone may not break symmetry in the first convolutional layer.
papers.abstract:
Deep neural networks are typically initialized with random weights, with
variances chosen to facilitate signal propagation and stable gradients. It is
also believed that diversity of features is an important property of these
initializations. We construct a deep convolutional network with identical
features by initializing almost all the weights to $0$. The architecture also
enables perfect signal propagation and stable gradients, and achieves high
accuracy on standard benchmarks. This indicates that random, diverse
initializations are \textit{not} necessary for training neural networks. An
essential element in training this network is a mechanism of symmetry breaking;
we study this phenomenon and find that standard GPU operations, which are
non-deterministic, can serve as a sufficient source of symmetry breaking to
enable training.

papers.title: A Renormalization Group Framework for Scale-Invariant Feature Learning in Deep Neural Networks (Student Abstract)
papers.research_question: How can renormalization group theory be applied to analyze and optimize hierarchical feature learning in deep neural networks, with a focus on scale invariance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a renormalization group framework for scale-invariant feature learning in deep neural networks, introducing scale-aware activation functions and RG-guided training to converge to fixed points.
papers.conclusion: The framework unifies deep learning and RG theory, enhancing interpretability and generalization through scale-invariant feature learning.
papers.key_findings:
Scale-aware activation functions enable scale covariance in neural network layers.
RG flow equations for network parameters are derived, linking learning dynamics to statistical physics.
Fixed points of RG flow correspond to scale-invariant feature representations.
RG-guided training procedure converges to these fixed points while minimizing loss.
Layer information decreases monotonically, indicating coarse-graining in hierarchical feature learning.
future_direction: Empirically validating the proposed framework through simulations.
papers.abstract: We propose a framework that uses renormalization group (RG) theory from statistical physics to analyze and optimize the hierarchical feature learning process in deep neural networks. Here, the layer-wise transformations in deep networks can be viewed as analogous to RG transformations, with each layer implementing a coarse-graining operation that extracts increasingly abstract features. We propose an approach to enforce scale invariance in neural networks, introduce scale-aware activation functions, and derive RG flow equations for network parameters. We show that our approach leads to fixed points corresponding to scale-invariant feature representations. Finally, we propose an RG-guided training procedure that converges to these fixed points while minimizing the loss function.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Efficient, probabilistic analysis of combinatorial neural codes
papers.research_question: How can combinatorial neural codes be efficiently and probabilistically analyzed to infer algebraic, geometric, and topological characteristics, and how do these characteristics relate to learning and experience in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper improves the computational complexity of analyzing combinatorial neural codes from factorial to quadratic time and introduces a probabilistic hypothesis testing framework, enabling efficient analysis of large neural codes from both artificial and biological neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Efficient and probabilistic analysis of combinatorial neural codes is feasible and provides insights into how internal representations change with learning and network depth.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method reduces the time complexity of computing the canonical form's generators from factorial to quadratic, enabling analysis of large neural codes.
Applied to simulated place cell data, the method correctly infers the number of holes in 2D navigation environments.
Applied to an MLP trained on MNIST, the method shows that internal representations become lower-dimensional and more spread out during training.
papers.limitation:
Assumes joint activity of neurons corresponds to common inputs or selectivity thereof.
Binarizes neural signals into 'on' and 'off' states.
future_direction: Performing causal inference tests on neural co-activations.
Considering polynomials over larger finite fields or extending methods to more continuous structures.
papers.abstract: Artificial and biological neural networks (ANNs and BNNs) can encode inputs in the form of combinations of individual neurons' activities. These combinatorial neural codes present a computational challenge for direct and efficient analysis due to their high dimensionality and often large volumes of data. Here we improve the computational complexity -- from factorial to quadratic time -- of direct algebraic methods previously applied to small examples and apply them to large neural codes generated by experiments. These methods provide a novel and efficient way of probing algebraic, geometric, and topological characteristics of combinatorial neural codes and provide insights into how such characteristics are related to learning and experience in neural networks. We introduce a procedure to perform hypothesis testing on the intrinsic features of neural codes using information geometry. We then apply these methods to neural activities from an ANN for image classification and a BNN for 2D navigation to, without observing any inputs or outputs, estimate the structure and dimensionality of the stimulus or task space. Additionally, we demonstrate how an ANN varies its internal representations across network depth and during learning.

papers.title: Emergent Riemannian geometry over learning discrete computations on continuous manifolds
papers.research_question: How do neural networks learn to perform discrete computations on continuous data manifolds?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Riemannian geometric framework showing that network computation decomposes into discretising continuous inputs and performing logical operations, with different learning regimes affecting geometry and generalization.
papers.conclusion: Specific Riemannian geometric structures emerge over learning in networks trained to perform discrete tasks on input data lying on continuous manifolds, deepening theoretical understanding of neural network computations.
papers.key_findings:
The Riemannian pullback metric becomes highly localized near class boundaries, reflecting the discretisation of the continuous input manifold.
Feature learning partitions computation into binarisation of inputs and discrete logical operations, and this structured geometry generalizes to unseen inputs, while lazy learning does not.
Noise during training decreases the curvature of the manifold, corresponding to the network learning a flatter posterior distribution of the output.
Rich learning regimes lead to low-dimensional, structured representational geometry with high curvature peaks, promoting generalization, while lazy regimes lead to high-dimensional, random geometry.
Linear networks learn task-specific geometries but cannot induce curvature, limiting their ability to exactly discretise inputs or perform complex Boolean operations.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to simple networks (multi-layer perceptrons) trained on hand-crafted input manifolds, not complex architectures or real-world data.
future_direction: Extend analyses to more complex architectures trained on real-world data.
Use toy models to understand how manifold structure influences sample complexity or generalization error.
Manipulate representational geometry via constraints on the metric during training to design models with specific invariances.
papers.abstract: Many tasks require mapping continuous input data (e.g. images) to discrete task outputs (e.g. class labels). Yet, how neural networks learn to perform such discrete computations on continuous data manifolds remains poorly understood. Here, we show that signatures of such computations emerge in the representational geometry of neural networks as they learn. By analysing the Riemannian pullback metric across layers of a neural network, we find that network computation can be decomposed into two functions: discretising continuous input features and performing logical operations on these discretised variables. Furthermore, we demonstrate how different learning regimes (rich vs. lazy) have contrasting metric and curvature structures, affecting the ability of the networks to generalise to unseen inputs. Overall, our work provides a geometric framework for understanding how neural networks learn to perform discrete computations on continuous manifolds.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters.
