Our work establishes the geometric origin of key training phenomena in DNNs and reveals a hierarchy of accuracy basins analogous to phases in statistical physics.

papers.title: Symmetry and Generalisation in Neural Approximations of Renormalisation Transformations
papers.research_question: What role do parameter symmetry and network expressivity play in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group transformation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a competition between symmetry constraints and expressivity in neural networks learning renormalization transformations, with overly complex or overconstrained models generalizing poorly. It extends a cumulant propagation framework from MLPs to GNNs to elucidate internal information processing.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that balancing symmetry and expressivity is crucial for generalization in neural networks learning physical transformations, and the cumulant propagation framework offers insight into their internal information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Symmetrically constrained weights in MLPs combined with nonlinear activations (e.g., quadratic) lead to poor generalization, as shown analytically.
Linear networks with symmetric weights generalize well, but adding nonlinearities (ReLU, quadratic) under symmetry constraints degrades generalization.
The independent node approximation for cumulant propagation in GNNs is limited, especially for higher-order cumulants, due to neglected correlations from message passing.
GNNs perform comparably to MLPs on simple two-node graphs but their inductive biases are not beneficial for tasks lacking structural complexity.
Networks with learnable spline activations and fixed weights generalize poorly, while training both weights and splines yields linear solutions that generalize well.
papers.limitation:
The independent node approximation for GNN cumulant propagation is crude and neglects important interactions induced by message passing and weight sharing.
The study is limited to simple network architectures (shallow MLPs and GNNs) and synthetic tasks.
future_direction: Extending the cumulant propagation framework to more complex architectures and tasks.
Investigating the role of symmetry breaking in hierarchical learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have proven enormously successful at using multiple layers of representation to learn relevant features of structured data. Encoding physical symmetries into these models can improve performance on difficult tasks, and recent work has motivated the principle of parameter symmetry breaking and restoration as a unifying mechanism underlying their hierarchical learning dynamics. We evaluate the role of parameter symmetry and network expressivity in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group (RG) transformation, using the central limit theorem (CLT) as a test case map. We consider simple multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and graph neural networks (GNNs), and vary weight symmetries and activation functions across architectures. Our results reveal a competition between symmetry constraints and expressivity, with overly complex or overconstrained models generalising poorly. We analytically demonstrate this poor generalisation behaviour for certain constrained MLP architectures by recasting the CLT as a cumulant recursion relation and making use of an established framework to propagate cumulants through MLPs. We also empirically validate an extension of this framework from MLPs to GNNs, elucidating the internal information processing performed by these more complex models. These findings offer new insight into the learning dynamics of symmetric networks and their limitations in modelling structured physical transformations.

papers.title: On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of a network architecture (via intertwiner groups) relate to the symmetries in the network's internal representations of data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces intertwiner groups to connect architectural symmetries with symmetries in internal representations, and shows that for ReLU networks, the activation basis is special for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intertwiner groups connect architectural symmetries to representation symmetries, and provide a justification for focusing on activation basis in ReLU networks for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Intertwiner groups describe weight space symmetries and propagate to symmetries in internal representations.
Stitching with GReLU transformations incurs a small accuracy penalty, indicating that much of the variation between networks can be accounted for by GReLU.
GReLU-Procrustes and GReLU-CKA are effective dissimilarity measures invariant to GReLU transformations.
For ReLU networks, interpretability is higher in the activation basis than in arbitrary linear combinations, but this is not the case for networks without ReLU.
papers.limitation:
The theory does not fully account for residual connections, as noted in remark 3.6.
Stitching with GReLU does not achieve full accuracy, indicating that internal representations are not perfectly aligned by permutations and scalings.
papers.abstract: Symmetry is a fundamental tool in the exploration of a broad range of complex systems. In machine learning symmetry has been explored in both models and data. In this paper we seek to connect the symmetries arising from the architecture of a family of models with the symmetries of that family's internal representation of data. We do this by calculating a set of fundamental symmetry groups, which we call the intertwiner groups of the model. We connect intertwiner groups to a model's internal representations of data through a range of experiments that probe similarities between hidden states across models with the same architecture. Our work suggests that the symmetries of a network are propagated into the symmetries in that network's representation of data, providing us with a better understanding of how architecture affects the learning and prediction process. Finally, we speculate that for ReLU networks, the intertwiner groups may provide a justification for the common practice of concentrating model interpretability exploration on the activation basis in hidden layers rather than arbitrary linear combinations thereof.

papers.title: Information Geometry of Evolution of Neural Network Parameters While Training
papers.research_question: How can information geometric measures (information length and velocity) be used to study the evolution of neural network parameters during training and identify overfitting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that information geometric measures (information length and velocity) can capture phase transition-like behavior during neural network training, and that transitions in these measures coincide with overfitting, providing a method to detect overfitting without using test data.
papers.conclusion: Information geometry provides a useful tool to study training dynamics and forecast overfitting without referring to test data, and the observed transitions resemble phase transitions in physical systems.
papers.key_findings:
Information length initially scales linearly with training steps and changes behavior when the model starts overfitting.
The second derivative of log L with respect to log t exhibits a local minimum that coincides with the onset of overfitting, acting as an independent indicator.
This behavior is observed across different optimizers (SGD, Adadelta), hyperparameters (learning rate, dropout, noise regularization), and datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10).
Increased regularization (dropout, noise) reduces the depth of the local minimum in the second derivative, correlating with reduced overfitting.
The observed transitions are mathematically analogous to thermodynamic phase transitions and show finite-size scaling behavior.
future_direction: A more quantitative investigation into the critical exponents of the phase transition-like behavior.
Extending the analysis to more complex behaviors exhibited by other optimizers and investigating why Adadelta behaves similarly to SGD.
Theoretical investigation into the universality of these behaviors.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are powerful tools capable of approximating any arbitrary mathematical function, but their interpretability remains limited, rendering them as black box models. To address this issue, numerous methods have been proposed to enhance the explainability and interpretability of ANNs. In this study, we introduce the application of information geometric framework to investigate phase transition-like behavior during the training of ANNs and relate these transitions to overfitting in certain models. The evolution of ANNs during training is studied by looking at the probability distribution of its parameters. Information geometry utilizing the principles of differential geometry, offers a unique perspective on probability and statistics by considering probability density functions as points on a Riemannian manifold. We create this manifold using a metric based on Fisher information to define a distance and a velocity. By parameterizing this distance and velocity with training steps, we study how the ANN evolves as training progresses. Utilizing standard datasets like MNIST, FMNIST and CIFAR-10, we observe a transition in the motion on the manifold while training the ANN and this transition is identified with over-fitting in the ANN models considered. The information geometric transitions observed is shown to be mathematically similar to the phase transitions in physics. Preliminary results showing finite-size scaling behavior is also provided. This work contributes to the development of robust tools for improving the explainability and interpretability of ANNs, aiding in our understanding of the variability of the parameters these complex models exhibit during training.

papers.title: Detection of Phase Transition via Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can neural networks detect phase transitions in physical systems without prior knowledge of the order parameter or critical temperature?
papers.core_contribution: A convolutional neural network can detect the phase transition of the 2D Ising model without prior knowledge, and a novel order parameter derived from the network's weight matrix can identify the critical temperature.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks, particularly CNNs, can capture features of phase transitions and can be used to define order parameters that identify critical temperatures in physical systems.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrix of the trained CNN shows a domain-like structure with a boundary near the critical temperature.
An order parameter Wsum(β) defined from the weight matrix can be used to extract the critical temperature via fitting.
The extracted critical temperatures for different lattice sizes are consistent with the exact value to within 2-8% accuracy.
The CNN's convolutional filters resemble a real-space renormalization group transformation, capturing local magnetization.
A fully connected neural network also detects the phase transition but with less accuracy than the CNN.
future_direction: Applying the neural network design to other statistical models and non-trivial phases.
papers.abstract:
We design a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) which studies correlation
between discretized inverse temperature and spin configuration of 2D Ising
model and show that it can find a feature of the phase transition without
teaching any a priori information for it. We also define a new order parameter
via the CNN and show that it provides well approximated critical inverse
temperature. In addition, we compare the activation functions for convolution
layer and find that the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is important to detect the
phase transition of 2D Ising model.

papers.title: Navigating the Latent Space Dynamics of Neural Models
papers.research_question: How can neural models, specifically autoencoders, be interpreted as dynamical systems, and what properties of the model and data can be revealed by the latent vector field and its attractors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that autoencoders implicitly define a latent vector field whose attractors encode model properties, enabling analysis of generalization and memorization, data-free probing of pretrained models, and out-of-distribution detection.
papers.conclusion: The latent vector field provides a novel and powerful representation for analyzing neural models, revealing internal properties and enabling applications like data-free probing and OOD detection.
papers.key_findings:
Autoencoders define a latent vector field whose attractors correspond to memorized data points or generalized representations, depending on regularization.
During training, the model transitions from memorization to generalization, which is reflected in the evolution of attractors.
Attractors computed from Gaussian noise can recover semantic information from pretrained vision foundation models without any input data.
Trajectories in the latent vector field can distinguish in-distribution from out-of-distribution samples, enabling OOD detection.
The memorization-generalization trade-off is controlled by regularization strength, such as bottleneck dimension.
papers.limitation: The method is primarily demonstrated on autoencoders; extension to other architectures (e.g., SSL models, LLMs) requires further analysis.
future_direction: Study latent vector fields in models beyond autoencoders, such as self-supervised learning models and large language models.
Investigate the impact of architectural elements (e.g., positional embeddings) on the latent dynamics.
Explore the connection between latent dynamics and reasoning in models.
papers.abstract: Neural networks transform high-dimensional data into compact, structured representations, often modeled as elements of a lower dimensional latent space. In this paper, we present an alternative interpretation of neural models as dynamical systems acting on the latent manifold. Specifically, we show that autoencoder models implicitly define a latent vector field on the manifold, derived by iteratively applying the encoding-decoding map, without any additional training. We observe that standard training procedures introduce inductive biases that lead to the emergence of attractor points within this vector field. Drawing on this insight, we propose to leverage the vector field as a representation for the network, providing a novel tool to analyze the properties of the model and the data. This representation enables to: (i) analyze the generalization and memorization regimes of neural models, even throughout training; (ii) extract prior knowledge encoded in the network's parameters from the attractors, without requiring any input data; (iii) identify out-of-distribution samples from their trajectories in the vector field. We further validate our approach on vision foundation models, showcasing the applicability and effectiveness of our method in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: High-dimensional manifold of solutions in neural networks: insights from statistical physics
papers.core_contribution: The paper reviews the statistical mechanics approach to neural networks, focusing on the perceptron model, and explains how the geometry of the solution space (manifold of solutions) changes with the size of the training set.
papers.key_findings:
The SAT/UNSAT transition separates a satisfiable phase where solutions exist from an unsatisfiable phase where the solution set is empty.
In the binary perceptron, typical solutions are isolated, but there exist subdominant, wide flat minima that are algorithmically accessible.
The local entropy transition marks a change in the geometry of solution regions and is connected to the onset of algorithmic hardness in binary models.
In the spherical negative perceptron, the solution space is star-shaped, with a kernel region from which any other solution can be reached via a zero-error geodesic path.
Linear mode connectivity between solutions can be characterized analytically, revealing the structure of the solution manifold.
papers.abstract: In these pedagogic notes I review the statistical mechanics approach to neural networks, focusing on the paradigmatic example of the perceptron architecture with binary an continuous weights, in the classification setting. I will review the Gardner's approach based on replica method and the derivation of the SAT/UNSAT transition in the storage setting. Then, I discuss some recent works that unveiled how the zero training error configurations are geometrically arranged, and how this arrangement changes as the size of the training set increases. I also illustrate how different regions of solution space can be explored analytically and how the landscape in the vicinity of a solution can be characterized. I give evidence how, in binary weight models, algorithmic hardness is a consequence of the disappearance of a clustered region of solutions that extends to very large distances. Finally, I demonstrate how the study of linear mode connectivity between solutions can give insights into the average shape of the solution manifold.

papers.title: Connecting Neural Models Latent Geometries with Relative Geodesic Representations
papers.research_question: How can we capture the transformations between representational spaces of neural models trained on similar data distributions by leveraging the differential-geometric structure of their latent spaces?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces relative geodesic representations, a method that captures the intrinsic geometry of neural model latent spaces via a pullback metric, enabling alignment and stitching of models across different architectures, pretraining schemes, and modalities.
papers.conclusion: Relative geodesic representations provide a powerful and general framework for connecting neural model latent spaces by capturing their intrinsic Riemannian geometry, enabling effective model alignment and stitching without fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Relative geodesic representations outperform baseline methods (e.g., relative cosine representations, linear/orthogonal alignment) in retrieval and model stitching tasks.
The method is sample-efficient, achieving high performance with few anchors, and robust to the choice of anchor set.
It effectively aligns representational spaces of models trained with different initializations, architectures, and objectives (e.g., autoencoders, classifiers, self-supervised models).
The proposed approximation of geodesic energy using straight lines in latent space is both efficient and accurate, preserving the rank order of true geodesic distances.
The method generalizes across diverse datasets (MNIST, CIFAR, ImageNet, etc.) and modalities, demonstrating its broad applicability.
papers.limitation: The approach may have limitations in scalability and computational efficiency, particularly when dealing with very high-dimensional latent spaces or when requiring many discretization steps.
future_direction: Extending the method to other modalities beyond vision.
Exploring more efficient approximations of the geodesic energy to improve scalability.
papers.abstract: Neural models learn representations of high-dimensional data on low-dimensional manifolds. Multiple factors, including stochasticities in the training process, model architectures, and additional inductive biases, may induce different representations, even when learning the same task on the same data. However, it has recently been shown that when a latent structure is shared between distinct latent spaces, relative distances between representations can be preserved, up to distortions. Building on this idea, we demonstrate that exploiting the differential-geometric structure of latent spaces of neural models, it is possible to capture precisely the transformations between representational spaces trained on similar data distributions. Specifically, we assume that distinct neural models parametrize approximately the same underlying manifold, and introduce a representation based on the pullback metric that captures the intrinsic structure of the latent space, while scaling efficiently to large models. We validate experimentally our method on model stitching and retrieval tasks, covering autoencoders and vision foundation discriminative models, across diverse architectures, datasets, and pretraining schemes.

papers.title: The geometry of hidden representations of large transformer models
papers.research_question: How do the geometric and statistical properties of hidden representations evolve across layers in large transformer models, and can the intrinsic dimension profile be used to identify layers with maximal semantic content?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension profile of hidden representations in large transformers has a characteristic shape (peak, plateau, etc.), and the layers with minimal intrinsic dimension correspond to those with maximal semantic content, providing an unsupervised strategy to identify optimal layers for downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Large transformers behave like sophisticated autoencoders, with an encoding phase (expansion and compression) and a decoding phase, and the low-ID representations in the intermediate layers are semantically rich.
papers.key_findings:
Representations evolve in distinct phases: an initial expansion (high ID), a compression phase (low ID), and a decoding phase.
The ID profile shows a peak in early layers, a plateau/low-ID region in intermediate layers, and sometimes a second peak in later layers.
Semantic information (e.g., protein remote homology, image class labels) is best encoded in the low-ID regions.
The ID profile can be used in an unsupervised manner to identify layers optimal for downstream learning tasks.
The geometric evolution is consistent across transformers trained on different data modalities (protein sequences and images).
papers.limitation:
The use of average pooling to handle variable-length sequences may affect the intrinsic dimension estimates.
Differences in ID profiles between models may be attributed to data modality, training objectives, and preprocessing choices.
The analysis of NLP representations is preliminary and not as extensive as for protein and image models.
future_direction: Analyzing the similarity of representations in ID minima with those from models trained in a supervised setting.
Further investigation of the second peak in iGPT models and its relation to the decoding phase.
Extending the geometric analysis to a broader range of NLP tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Large transformers are powerful architectures used for self-supervised data analysis across various data types, including protein sequences, images, and text. In these models, the semantic structure of the dataset emerges from a sequence of transformations between one representation and the next. We characterize the geometric and statistical properties of these representations and how they change as we move through the layers. By analyzing the intrinsic dimension (ID) and neighbor composition, we find that the representations evolve similarly in transformers trained on protein language tasks and image reconstruction tasks. In the first layers, the data manifold expands, becoming high-dimensional, and then contracts significantly in the intermediate layers. In the last part of the model, the ID remains approximately constant or forms a second shallow peak. We show that the semantic information of the dataset is better expressed at the end of the first peak, and this phenomenon can be observed across many models trained on diverse datasets. Based on our findings, we point out an explicit strategy to identify, without supervision, the layers that maximize semantic content: representations at intermediate layers corresponding to a relative minimum of the ID profile are more suitable for downstream learning tasks.

papers.title: Representation Mechanics: Invariant-Governed Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection achieve generalization by learning and preserving invariants, as evidenced by early phase transitions (the Platonic Spike)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Representation Mechanics, showing that neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection can achieve generalization by learning invariants, as evidenced by the Platonic Spike (early phase transition where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that invariant-preserving inductive bias is sufficient for rule learning and that constructing reliable AI requires respecting the mechanics of representation (treating embeddings as physical objects with inertia, boundaries, and elasticity).
papers.key_findings:
Set-valued weights with learned selection lead to early phase transitions (Platonic Spike) where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy.
Classical activations (e.g., GELU, ELU, ReLU) interfere with basin preservation and cause overfitting or boundary erosion.
Basin preservation via path freezing can prevent catastrophic forgetting by maintaining separatrix integrity.
The Surgical Clutch mechanism allows for invariant maintenance under continual learning by dynamically routing gradients.
The architecture achieves high accuracy on synthetic logic and language tasks without relying on n-gram statistics.
papers.limitation: The current work uses explicit rule contexts, which may not be available in all domains, and the architecture has not yet been tested at scale.
future_direction: Testing the architecture at scale
Exploring amplification strategies (more branches, hierarchical scoring, contrastive loss)
Extending to domains without explicit rule contexts
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> We present Representation Mechanics, a theoretical and empirical framework characterizing learning in invariant-governed domains. We demonstrate that neural networks with set-valued operations (discrete potentials {-W, 0, +W}) and learned selection exhibit sharp phase transitions to generalization without pretraining. The Platonic Spike (Early Phase Transition)—where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy in early epochs—signals the discovery of structural invariants before instance memorization. We validate these findings on controlled synthetic tasks (spiral classification, closed-world logic, declarative language) to isolate geometric mechanics from natural language statistical confounds. We contrast this Form-First paradigm with diffusion-dominated learning and define the conditions (Basin Preservation and Friction Set tracking) required to maintain these invariants under continual learning pressure. Our results suggest that restricting representational freedom via discrete potentials is not a limitation but a necessary inductive bias for rule-consistent generalization.

papers.title: Symmetry in language statistics shapes the geometry of model representations
papers.research_question: Why do geometric structures (circles, loops, manifolds) arise in the internal representations of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that translation symmetry in pairwise co-occurrence statistics of natural language explains the emergence of geometric structures (e.g., circles, manifolds) in the internal representations of language models.
papers.conclusion: Representational manifolds have a universal origin: symmetry in the statistics of natural data.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical observation of representation manifolds (circles, loops) and linear coordinate decoding in shallow word embedding models like word2vec.
Evidence that words embodying a continuous latent concept have pairwise co-occurrence statistics that exhibit translation symmetry.
Analytical expressions that predict the representational geometry directly from these translation symmetric statistics.
Validation that the predicted representational structure is present and stable in both word embedding models and deep transformer-based models.
Theoretical and empirical demonstration that representation manifolds are robust to significant perturbations in co-occurrence statistics, explained by collective effects involving many words.
papers.abstract: Although learned representations underlie neural networks' success, their fundamental properties remain poorly understood. A striking example is the emergence of simple geometric structures in LLM representations: for example, calendar months organize into a circle, years form a smooth one-dimensional manifold, and cities' latitudes and longitudes can be decoded by a linear probe. We show that the statistics of language exhibit a translation symmetry -- e.g., the co-occurrence probability of two months depends only on the time interval between them -- and we prove that the latter governs the aforementioned geometric structures in high-dimensional word embedding models. Moreover, we find that these structures persist even when the co-occurrence statistics are strongly perturbed (for example, by removing all sentences in which two months appear together) and at moderate embedding dimension. We show that this robustness naturally emerges if the co-occurrence statistics are collectively controlled by an underlying continuous latent variable. We empirically validate this theoretical framework in word embedding models, text embedding models, and large language models.

papers.title: How does training shape the Riemannian geometry of neural network representations?
papers.research_question: How does training shape the Riemannian geometry induced by neural network feature maps?
papers.core_contribution: Training shapes the Riemannian geometry of neural network feature maps to magnify local areas along decision boundaries, a phenomenon observed in both supervised and self-supervised learning.
papers.conclusion: Training molds the Riemannian geometry of neural network representations to magnify areas along decision boundaries, providing a preliminary picture of how feature learning shapes geometry and opening avenues for understanding geometric inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
At infinite width, neural networks with random parameters induce highly symmetric metrics on input space.
Feature learning breaks this symmetry: networks trained for classification learn to expand the volume element (local area magnification) near decision boundaries.
This area expansion near decision boundaries holds for shallow networks on toy tasks, deep ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-10, and in self-supervised learning with Barlow Twins.
The volume element is largest near decision boundaries and smallest within class regions.
The contrast in volume element between decision boundaries and class regions increases with network depth.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on toy tasks with two-dimensional input domains or low-dimensional slices through high-dimensional domains, limiting visualization of the full geometry.
Computational constraints, particularly for computing anisotropic measures like the Ricci scalar, and numerical challenges in curvature estimation.
The approach does not apply directly to networks with ReLU activation functions due to non-differentiability, requiring analysis of piecewise-constant magnification factors across activation regions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient and numerically stable algorithms for computing geometric quantities like curvature in state-of-the-art architectures.
Investigating when the flexible, nonlinear form of feature learning that reshapes embedding curvature is necessary for generalization, compared to linear methods.
Applying the geometric analysis to pre-trained networks, including those for which training classes are unknown, and to differentiable approximations of biological neural networks.
papers.abstract: In machine learning, there is a long history of trying to build neural networks that can learn from fewer example data by baking in strong geometric priors. However, it is not always clear a priori what geometric constraints are appropriate for a given task. Here, we explore the possibility that one can uncover useful geometric inductive biases by studying how training molds the Riemannian geometry induced by unconstrained neural network feature maps. We first show that at infinite width, neural networks with random parameters induce highly symmetric metrics on input space. This symmetry is broken by feature learning: networks trained to perform classification tasks learn to magnify local areas along decision boundaries. This holds in deep networks trained on high-dimensional image classification tasks, and even in self-supervised representation learning. These results begin to elucidate how training shapes the geometry induced by unconstrained neural network feature maps, laying the groundwork for an understanding of this richly nonlinear form of feature learning.

papers.title: Dynamic neuron approach to deep neural networks: Decoupling neurons for renormalization group analysis
papers.research_question: How can we reformulate the cost function of deep neural networks to reveal translational symmetry and enable the application of renormalization group transformations and analysis of critical phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the dynamic neuron approach (DNA), which reformulates the cost function of deep neural networks by treating neurons as dynamic degrees of freedom, revealing translational symmetry and enabling the application of renormalization group transformations to analyze critical phenomena.
papers.conclusion: The dynamic neuron approach provides a new framework for analyzing deep neural networks using statistical physics, revealing translational symmetry and enabling renormalization group transformations and critical phenomena analysis.
papers.key_findings:
The dynamic neuron approach (DNA) reformulates the DNN cost function by introducing neurons as dynamic degrees of freedom, simplifying interactions and revealing approximate translational symmetry.
Using DNA, the renormalization group transformation can be applied to DNNs, leading to a renormalized system with reduced depth and new constraints.
In a simplified DNN example with one neuron per layer, the RG transformation yields fixed points and scaling laws, indicating potential critical phenomena.
Monte Carlo simulations show that the correlation functions of the DNA system closely resemble those of the original DNN, validating DNA as a theoretical approximation.
The DNA Hamiltonian, under certain assumptions, resembles a spin glass model, connecting DNN training to statistical physics models.
papers.limitation:
The simple example with assumptions (one neuron per layer, single data point, Heaviside activation, discrete weights) may oversimplify and differ from actual DNNs.
The DNA introduces a large number of dynamic neurons (LMN), making it computationally infeasible for practical applications.
future_direction: Develop theoretical tools for inference to study neural scaling laws.
Develop optimization methods to make DNA practically feasible.
papers.abstract: Deep neural network architectures often consist of repetitive structural elements. We introduce an approach that reveals these patterns and can be broadly applied to the study of deep learning. Similarly to how a power strip helps untangle and organize complex cable connections, this approach treats neurons as additional degrees of freedom in interactions, simplifying the structure and enhancing the intuitive understanding of interactions within deep neural networks. Furthermore, it reveals the translational symmetry of deep neural networks, which simplifies the application of the renormalization group transformation, a method that effectively analyzes the scaling behavior of the system. By utilizing translational symmetry and renormalization group transformations, we can analyze critical phenomena. This approach may open new avenues for studying deep neural networks using statistical physics.

papers.title: Learning through atypical phase transitions in overparameterized neural networks
papers.research_question: How does overparameterization affect the geometrical structure of minima in non-convex neural networks, and how does this relate to learning and generalization performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that overparameterized non-convex neural networks exhibit two phase transitions: the interpolation threshold and the Local Entropy transition, and that efficient learning algorithms sample from wide, atypical minima with good generalization, despite typical minima being sharp and numerous.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that atypical phase transitions driven by rare, wide minima are key to understanding learning in overparameterized non-convex networks.
papers.key_findings:
There are two phase transitions: the interpolation threshold (where solutions appear) and the Local Entropy transition (where wide minima appear).
Typical solutions are sharp and isolated, with poor generalization.
Atypical solutions are wide and dense, with good generalization, and are sampled by efficient algorithms.
The Local Entropy transition is the relevant one for learning.
Numerical experiments on various architectures confirm the theoretical predictions.
future_direction: Conduct in-depth numerical studies of large deep networks.
Corroborate results with rigorous bounds for more general data distributions.
Theoretical confirmation that dynamics of a broad class of algorithms is attracted to these structures.
papers.abstract: Current deep neural networks are highly overparameterized (up to billions of connection weights) and nonlinear. Yet they can fit data almost perfectly through variants of gradient descent algorithms and achieve unexpected levels of prediction accuracy without overfitting. These are formidable results that defy predictions of statistical learning and pose conceptual challenges for nonconvex optimization. In this paper, we use methods from statistical physics of disordered systems to analytically study the computational fallout of overparameterization in nonconvex binary neural network models, trained on data generated from a structurally simpler but "hidden" network. As the number of connection weights increases, we follow the changes of the geometrical structure of different minima of the error loss function and relate them to learning and generalization performance. A first transition happens at the so-called interpolation point, when solutions begin to exist (perfect fitting becomes possible). This transition reflects the properties of typical solutions, which however are in sharp minima and hard to sample. After a gap, a second transition occurs, with the discontinuous appearance of a different kind of "atypical" structures: wide regions of the weight space that are particularly solution dense and have good generalization properties. The two kinds of solutions coexist, with the typical ones being exponentially more numerous, but empirically we find that efficient algorithms sample the atypical, rare ones. This suggests that the atypical phase transition is the relevant one for learning. The results of numerical tests with realistic networks on observables suggested by the theory are consistent with this scenario.

papers.title: Phase transitions from linear to nonlinear information processing in neural networks
papers.research_question: How does the information processing capacity of echo state networks change as a function of nonlinearity and network size, and does a discontinuous phase transition occur in the limit of infinite nodes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a phase transition from linear to nonlinear information processing in echo state networks, which becomes discontinuous in the limit of infinite network size and is distinct from the conventional order-to-chaos transition.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals a phase transition from linear to nonlinear information processing in neural networks, which may represent a new class of nonequilibrium phase transitions in high-dimensional dynamical systems.
papers.key_findings:
For small input weight standard deviation, the network operates in an approximately linear regime with limited information processing capacity.
Beyond a critical input weight standard deviation, the capacity increases rapidly, and the transition sharpens as the network size grows, indicating a discontinuous jump in the infinite-node limit.
The critical nonlinearity scales with noise intensity as σ_in,0 ∝ σ_ξ^{1/3}, implying that even infinitesimally weak nonlinearity can drive the system into the nonlinear regime in the absence of noise.
The transition is fundamentally different from the order-to-chaos transition, which typically reduces capacity.
The scaling exponent for the critical nonlinearity is determined by the order of the leading nonlinear term in the activation function's Taylor expansion.
papers.limitation:
At present, we do not have a theoretical explanation for the phase transition.
Numerical round-off errors can induce an artificial transition when noise is absent, acting as an implicit noise source.
future_direction: Further investigations with larger networks are required to conclusively determine the scaling exponents and universality of the transition.
Theoretical explanation of the phase transition is needed.
Understanding these transitions may reveal novel universality classes in nonequilibrium phase transitions.
papers.abstract: We investigate a phase transition from linear to nonlinear information processing in echo state networks, a widely used framework in reservoir computing. The network consists of randomly connected recurrent nodes perturbed by a noise and the output is obtained through linear regression on the network states. By varying the standard deviation of the input weights, we systematically control the nonlinearity of the network. For small input standard deviations, the network operates in an approximately linear regime, resulting in limited information processing capacity. However, beyond a critical threshold, the capacity increases rapidly, and this increase becomes sharper as the network size grows. Our results indicate the presence of a discontinuous transition in the limit of infinitely many nodes. This transition is fundamentally different from the conventional order-to-chaos transition in neural networks, which typically leads to a loss of long-term predictability and a decline in the information processing capacity. Furthermore, we establish a scaling law relating the critical nonlinearity to the noise intensity, which implies that the critical nonlinearity vanishes in the absence of noise.

papers.title: Exponential expressivity in deep neural networks through transient chaos
papers.research_question: What is the nature of signal propagation in generic deep neural networks with random weights, and how does depth contribute to exponential expressivity that shallow networks cannot achieve?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that deep random neural networks in a chaotic phase exhibit exponential growth in the curvature of simple manifolds with depth, formalizing the idea of disentangling and proving shallow networks cannot efficiently compute such functions.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks in the chaotic phase can efficiently compute highly expressive functions that shallow networks cannot, and the Riemannian geometry framework quantifies the disentangling of curved input manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
Deep networks in the chaotic phase exhibit exponential growth in the global curvature of manifolds with depth, but not width.
An order-to-chaos expressivity phase transition occurs depending on weight and bias statistics.
Shallow networks cannot achieve exponential expressivity; their Euclidean length grows at most as the square root of width.
Decision boundaries become exponentially curved with depth when backpropagated to the input layer.
The theoretical framework applies to arbitrary nonlinearities and provides a unifying basis for deep expressivity.
future_direction: Using the analysis as a null model to understand what is special about trained networks.
Studying the geometry of the graph of deep network functions as a Riemannian manifold to uncover secrets of deep learning.
papers.abstract: We combine Riemannian geometry with the mean field theory of high dimensional chaos to study the nature of signal propagation in generic, deep neural networks with random weights. Our results reveal an order-to-chaos expressivity phase transition, with networks in the chaotic phase computing nonlinear functions whose global curvature grows exponentially with depth but not width. We prove this generic class of deep random functions cannot be efficiently computed by any shallow network, going beyond prior work restricted to the analysis of single functions. Moreover, we formalize and quantitatively demonstrate the long conjectured idea that deep networks can disentangle highly curved manifolds in input space into flat manifolds in hidden space. Our theoretical analysis of the expressive power of deep networks broadly applies to arbitrary nonlinearities, and provides a quantitative underpinning for previously abstract notions about the geometry of deep functions.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Probing Biological and Artificial Neural Networks with Task-dependent Neural Manifolds
papers.research_question: How do different learning objectives (supervised vs. unsupervised) lead to differences in the organizational strategies of neural networks, and how can neural population geometry bridge mechanistic and normative theories?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a geometric framework based on manifold capacity theory and manifold alignment analysis to reveal differences in organizational strategies between supervised and unsupervised neural networks, and shows that these geometric properties are associated with computational performance such as regression.
papers.conclusion: Geometric analyses at the representation level can reveal differences in organizational strategies of neural networks with distinct objectives, and these geometric properties are associated with computational performance, offering a bridge between mechanistic and normative theories.
papers.key_findings:
Supervised DNNs achieve higher manifold classification capacity by shrinking their object manifolds more than unsupervised DNNs.
Unsupervised DNNs have more aligned object manifolds in the representational space compared to supervised DNNs.
Stronger manifold alignment is associated with lower regression error, suggesting an advantage for learning aligned representations.
The geometry of neural representations in macaque visual cortex is more similar to unsupervised DNNs than to supervised DNNs.
Task-dependent manifold analysis reveals organizational structure that is missed by traditional methods like representational similarity analysis (RSA).
papers.limitation: MCT focuses on single manifold geometry, while MAA only addresses a fraction of the relations across manifolds, leaving some underlying mechanisms open.
future_direction: Develop rigorous theoretical connections between geometry and regression performance.
Explore other benefits of manifold alignment, such as explaining pretraining effectiveness.
Extend geometric metrics to compare DNNs and the brain in more detail.
papers.abstract: Recently, growth in our understanding of the computations performed in both biological and artificial neural networks has largely been driven by either low-level mechanistic studies or global normative approaches. However, concrete methodologies for bridging the gap between these levels of abstraction remain elusive. In this work, we investigate the internal mechanisms of neural networks through the lens of neural population geometry, aiming to provide understanding at an intermediate level of abstraction, as a way to bridge that gap. Utilizing manifold capacity theory (MCT) from statistical physics and manifold alignment analysis (MAA) from high-dimensional statistics, we probe the underlying organization of task-dependent manifolds in deep neural networks and macaque neural recordings. Specifically, we quantitatively characterize how different learning objectives lead to differences in the organizational strategies of these models and demonstrate how these geometric analyses are connected to the decodability of task-relevant information. These analyses present a strong direction for bridging mechanistic and normative theories in neural networks through neural population geometry, potentially opening up many future research avenues in both machine learning and neuroscience.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do abstract representations emerge in neural networks? Specifically, the paper investigates whether abstract representations are guaranteed to appear in feedforward networks trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical theory proving that abstract representations are guaranteed to emerge in the hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables, and develops a mean-field optimization framework to analyze such representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that abstract representations emerge naturally in neural networks trained on tasks with latent variables, providing a mathematical explanation for similar observations in neuroscience and machine learning, and offers a general framework for understanding representation geometry in task-optimized networks.
papers.key_findings:
For whitened and target-aligned inputs, ReLU networks develop abstract representations with parallelism score (PS) equal to 1 at global minima.
The optimal representation kernel takes the form K = a*11^T + b*K_Y, where K_Y is the output kernel.
The emergence of abstract representations is robust to the choice of activation function, holding for two broad classes of nonlinearities: threshold functions and odd functions.
The theory extends to multi-element classes (n ≥ 2) and deep feedforward architectures.
The framework provides a mean-field description where the optimal preactivation distribution satisfies a self-consistent condition.
papers.limitation:
The theory is limited to feedforward networks trained on tasks with binary latent variables and assumes the network reaches a global minimum.
The analysis assumes specific input geometries (whitened or target-aligned inputs) and may not cover all possible input structures.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other architectures such as ResNet and transformer models.
Analyze learning dynamics in networks trained with biological learning rules.
Investigate the Platonic representation hypothesis using the developed mathematical toolkit.
papers.abstract: Recent experiments reveal that task-relevant variables are often encoded in approximately orthogonal subspaces of the neural activity space. These disentangled low-dimensional representations are observed in multiple brain areas and across different species, and are typically the result of a process of abstraction that supports simple forms of out-of-distribution generalization. The mechanisms by which such geometries emerge remain poorly understood, and the mechanisms that have been investigated are typically unsupervised (e.g., based on variational auto-encoders). Here, we show mathematically that abstract representations of latent variables are guaranteed to appear in the last hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when they are trained on tasks that depend directly on these latent variables. These abstract representations reflect the structure of the desired outputs or the semantics of the input stimuli. To investigate the neural representations that emerge in these networks, we develop an analytical framework that maps the optimization over the network weights into a mean-field problem over the distribution of neural preactivations. Applying this framework to a finite-width ReLU network, we find that its hidden layer exhibits an abstract representation at all global minima of the task objective. We further extend these analyses to two broad families of activation functions and deep feedforward architectures, demonstrating that abstract representations naturally arise in all these scenarios. Together, these results provide an explanation for the widely observed abstract representations in both the brain and artificial neural networks, as well as a mathematically tractable toolkit for understanding the emergence of different kinds of representations in task-optimized, feature-learning network models.

papers.title: Emergence of Quantised Representations Isolated to Anisotropic Functions
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of activation functions (discrete vs. continuous) influence the emergence and organization of discrete representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that activation functions defined by discrete algebraic symmetries (e.g., permutation-equivariance) induce a quantizing inductive bias, leading to discrete, symmetry-organized clusters in representations, whereas functions with continuous symmetries (e.g., orthogonal-equivariance) preserve more continuous representations.
papers.conclusion: The symmetry properties of activation functions act as a strong inductive bias, with discrete symmetries leading to quantized representations and continuous symmetries preserving continuity, implying that many observed interpretability structures are not fundamental but arise from specific architectural choices.
papers.key_findings:
Discrete symmetry-defined activation functions (e.g., standard tanh) cause representations to cluster around distinguished directions, leading to quantized, discrete structures.
Continuous symmetry-defined activation functions (e.g., isotropic tanh) do not induce such task-agnostic clustering, resulting in more continuous representations.
The observed quantisation effect correlates with a measurable increase in reconstruction error, suggesting potential pathological consequences.
The Privileged-Plane Projective Method (PPP) is introduced as a tool for high-fidelity visualization of representational geometry, preserving both angular and magnitude information.
The findings suggest that many interpretability phenomena (e.g., grandmother neurons, discrete coding) may be contingent on the choice of anisotropic functional forms rather than fundamental to deep learning.
papers.limitation:
The performance analysis (reconstruction error) is preliminary, as the isotropic activation functions are placeholder designs not optimized for performance.
The study is conducted on relatively small autoencoder models; the findings may not generalize directly to larger, more complex architectures like transformers.
future_direction: Further investigation into the pathological implications of function-driven quantisation, such as effects on adversarial robustness and representational capacity.
Exploration of isotropic functional forms in larger model architectures and their potential performance benefits.
Development of a more comprehensive taxonomy of symmetry-defined functional forms and their representational biases.
papers.abstract: Presented is a novel methodology for determining representational structure, which builds upon the existing Spotlight Resonance method. This new tool is used to gain insight into how discrete representations can emerge and organise in autoencoder models, through a controlled ablation study that alters only the activation function. Using this technique, the validity of whether function-driven symmetries can act as implicit inductive biases on representations is determined. Representations are found to tend to discretise when the activation functions are defined through a discrete algebraic permutation-equivariant symmetry. In contrast, they remain continuous under a continuous algebraic orthogonal-equivariant definition. This confirms the hypothesis that the symmetries of network primitives can carry unintended inductive biases, leading to task-independent artefactual structures in representations. The discrete symmetry of contemporary forms is shown to be a strong predictor for the production of symmetry-organised discrete representations emerging from otherwise continuous distributions -- a quantisation effect. This motivates further reassessment of functional forms in common usage due to such unintended consequences. Moreover, this supports a general causal model for a mode in which discrete representations may form, and could constitute a prerequisite for downstream interpretability phenomena, including grandmother neurons, discrete coding schemes, general linear features and a type of Superposition. Hence, this tool and proposed mechanism for the influence of functional form on representations may provide insights into interpretability research. Finally, preliminary results indicate that quantisation of representations correlates with a measurable increase in reconstruction error, reinforcing previous conjectures that this collapse can be detrimental.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: On the emergence of simplex symmetry in the final and penultimate layers of neural network classifiers
papers.research_question: Why do neural network classifiers exhibit simplex symmetry (neural collapse) in the final and penultimate layers, and under what conditions does this occur?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides an analytical explanation for the emergence of simplex symmetry (neural collapse) in the final and penultimate layers of neural network classifiers under certain conditions, and shows that this collapse may not occur in shallow networks or when the data does not allow it.
papers.conclusion: Simplex symmetry emerges in deep neural network classifiers when the hypothesis class is sufficiently expressive and the optimization respects certain geometric constraints, but this collapse may not occur in shallower networks or under different data geometries.
papers.key_findings:
Under assumptions of high expressivity and norm constraints, the optimal configuration in the final layer maps each class to a vertex of a regular simplex.
Similarly, in the penultimate layer, the optimal configuration also forms a regular simplex when the classifier is composed of a linear transformation and a highly expressive function.
For shallow neural networks (two-layer networks) trained by gradient descent, the classifier may not collapse each class to a single point, as demonstrated in two examples.
The analysis is independent of the number of data points and the weights of different classes in the final layer toy model, but interactions in shallow networks depend on class probabilities.
The simplex geometry in the penultimate layer specifically relies on Euclidean geometry, while the final layer result holds for various ℓp-norms.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis raises the question of whether the simplex configuration is desirable or merely optimal in a hypothesis class too large to allow statistical generalization bounds.
The analysis applies to norm-constrained energy minimizers, not necessarily to training dynamics, and the dynamics would depend on the precise function model.
The results for the penultimate layer rely on Euclidean geometry, which may not be justified in deeper layers.
future_direction: Investigate whether neural collapse occurs on random data sets or real data sets with randomly permuted labels.
Determine if neural collapse occurs on test data or only on training data.
Explore whether neural collapse is observed for ReLU activation functions, or only for activation functions which tend to a limit at positive and negative infinity.
papers.abstract: A recent numerical study observed that neural network classifiers enjoy a large degree of symmetry in the penultimate layer. Namely, if $h(x) = Af(x) +b$ where $A$ is a linear map and $f$ is the output of the penultimate layer of the network (after activation), then all data points $x_{i, 1}, \dots, x_{i, N_i}$ in a class $C_i$ are mapped to a single point $y_i$ by $f$ and the points $y_i$ are located at the vertices of a regular $k-1$-dimensional standard simplex in a high-dimensional Euclidean space. We explain this observation analytically in toy models for highly expressive deep neural networks. In complementary examples, we demonstrate rigorously that even the final output of the classifier $h$ is not uniform over data samples from a class $C_i$ if $h$ is a shallow network (or if the deeper layers do not bring the data samples into a convenient geometric configuration).

papers.title: Task structure and nonlinearity jointly determine learned representational geometry
papers.research_question: How do activation function, input structure, and output structure jointly determine the learned representational geometry in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The activation function (Tanh vs ReLU) has a strong impact on learned representational geometry: Tanh networks align representations with target output geometry, while ReLU networks retain more input geometry, due to differences in symmetry and asymptotic behavior.
papers.conclusion: The activation function plays a crucial role in determining whether learned representations align more with target output geometry or input geometry, shedding light on the interplay between input-output geometry, nonlinearity, and learned representations.
papers.key_findings:
Tanh networks learn representations that reflect the structure of target outputs, while ReLU networks retain more information about input structure.
This difference is consistent across a broad class of parameterized tasks with varying input-output alignment.
The difference arises from asymmetric asymptotic behavior of ReLU leading to feature neuron specialization, while Tanh's symmetry causes neurons to inherit task label structure.
When target outputs are low-dimensional, Tanh networks produce more disentangled representations than ReLU networks.
The findings generalize to multi-layer networks and convolutional networks on image classification tasks.
future_direction: Investigate the progression of target/input alignment across layers in multi-layer networks for easy vs. hard tasks.
In-depth characterization of the effect of high input noise on target alignment in ReLU networks.
papers.abstract: The utility of a learned neural representation depends on how well its geometry supports performance in downstream tasks. This geometry depends on the structure of the inputs, the structure of the target outputs, and the architecture of the network. By studying the learning dynamics of networks with one hidden layer, we discovered that the network's activation function has an unexpectedly strong impact on the representational geometry: Tanh networks tend to learn representations that reflect the structure of the target outputs, while ReLU networks retain more information about the structure of the raw inputs. This difference is consistently observed across a broad class of parameterized tasks in which we modulated the degree of alignment between the geometry of the task inputs and that of the task labels. We analyzed the learning dynamics in weight space and show how the differences between the networks with Tanh and ReLU nonlinearities arise from the asymmetric asymptotic behavior of ReLU, which leads feature neurons to specialize for different regions of input space. By contrast, feature neurons in Tanh networks tend to inherit the task label structure. Consequently, when the target outputs are low dimensional, Tanh networks generate neural representations that are more disentangled than those obtained with a ReLU nonlinearity. Our findings shed light on the interplay between input-output geometry, nonlinearity, and learned representations in neural networks.

papers.title: Scale-Agnostic Kolmogorov-Arnold Geometry in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Whether Kolmogorov-Arnold geometry persists in realistic high-dimensional settings and what spatial properties this geometry exhibits.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Kolmogorov-Arnold geometry emerges spontaneously in MLPs trained on MNIST and is scale-agnostic across spatial scales and training procedures.
papers.conclusion: KAG is scale-agnostic and emerges spontaneously in neural networks, suggesting it may be a fundamental property of learned representations with implications for understanding learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
KAG emerges during training in 2-layer MLPs on MNIST, with stronger signatures in larger networks.
KAG appears consistently across spatial scales from local neighborhoods to the full image.
The scale-agnostic property is robust to training procedures, appearing in both standard and augmented training.
Augmented training yields lower participation ratios, indicating reduced geometric frustration.
KAG signatures are stronger in the first hidden layer compared to the second.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to MNIST, a simple grayscale recognition task.
Networks are shallow (two hidden layers), and it's unclear if patterns persist in modern deep architectures.
The rotation ratio metric has higher baseline variance, making it less reliable for primary claims.
future_direction: Moving beyond correlation to causation through frustration experiments and explicit regularization.
Extending analysis to modern architectures like CNNs, ResNets, and attention-based models.
Scaling to larger datasets such as ImageNet or language modeling datasets.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Freedman and Mulligan demonstrated that shallow multilayer perceptrons spontaneously develop Kolmogorov-Arnold geometric (KAG) structure during training on synthetic three-dimensional tasks. However, it remained unclear whether this phenomenon persists in realistic high-dimensional settings and what spatial properties this geometry exhibits. We extend KAG analysis to MNIST digit classification (784 dimensions) using 2-layer MLPs with systematic spatial analysis at multiple scales. We find that KAG emerges during training and appears consistently across spatial scales, from local 7-pixel neighborhoods to the full 28x28 image. This scale-agnostic property holds across different training procedures: both standard training and training with spatial augmentation produce the same qualitative pattern. These findings reveal that neural networks spontaneously develop organized, scale-invariant geometric structure during learning on realistic high-dimensional data.

papers.title: The Geometry of Machine Learning Models
papers.research_question: How can machine learning models be analyzed through the geometric properties of their induced partitions, and how can this geometric perspective enable new regularization and refinement techniques?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a mathematical framework for analyzing machine learning models through the geometry of their induced partitions, enabling geometric regularization and new model refinement tools like extended Laplacians and simplicial splines.
papers.conclusion: The geometric framework offers new approaches to model interpretation, regularization, and diagnostic tools for understanding learning dynamics, though experimental validation remains for future work.
papers.key_findings:
Machine learning models can be represented as Riemannian simplicial complexes that capture geometric properties of partitions such as cell volumes, boundary areas, and dihedral angles.
Geometric regularization can directly penalize problematic spatial configurations like extreme volume disparities and sharp angles at boundaries.
Extended Laplacians and simplicial splines provide new tools for model refinement by incorporating higher-order geometric relationships beyond simple adjacency.
Data distribution induces effective geometric curvature in model partitions, which can be measured through discrete curvature measures and statistical Ricci curvature.
A differential forms approach makes geometric computations tractable for neural networks by tracking volume transformations through layers via pullback operations.
papers.limitation: The framework is theoretical and requires experimental validation.
future_direction: Experimental validation of the theoretical insights.
Scaling the geometric computations to very large networks.
Exploring theoretical questions bridging abstract mathematics and practical machine learning, such as how geometric invariants relate to generalization and robustness.
